So these are two signs and two proofs. Al-Mahdawī said: the benefit of the verse is that He informed them that Jesus (peace be upon him) would speak to them in the cradle and live until he spoke to them in maturity, since it was customary that one who spoke in the cradle did not live.

Al-Zajjāj said: "and in maturity" means "and he shall speak to people in maturity". Al-Farrāʾ and al-Akhfash said: it is conjoined to "honoured". It was said: the meaning is, and he shall speak to people as a small child and as a mature man. Ibn Jurayj related from Mujāhid, who said: the kahl is the forbearing one. Al-Naḥḥās said: this is not known in the language; the kahl according to the people of the language is only one who approaches forty. Some of them said: one is called a youth (ḥadath) until sixteen years, then a young man (shābb) until thirty-two, then he becomes a kahl at thirty-three; so said al-Akhfash.

and of the righteous is conjoined to "honoured", that is, and he is of the righteous worshippers. Abū Bakr ibn Abī Shaybah mentioned: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Idrīs related to us, from Ḥuṣayn, from Hilāl ibn Yisāf, who said: None spoke in the cradle except three: Jesus, the companion of Joseph, and the companion of Jurayj. Thus he said: "and the companion of Joseph". It is in the Ṣaḥīḥ of Muslim from Abū Hurayrah, from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), who said: "None spoke in the cradle except three: Jesus son of Mary, the companion of Jurayj, and the companion of the tyrant; and while an infant was suckling from his mother…", and he mentioned the ḥadīth in its full length. There has come from the ḥadīth of Ṣuhayb, in the story of the Trench (al-Ukhdūd): "that a woman was brought to be cast into the fire for her faith, and with her was a child", and in other than the book of Muslim: "suckling, and she hung back from falling into it, and the boy said: O mother, be steadfast, for you are upon the truth." Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: six spoke in the cradle: the witness of Joseph, the child of the hairdresser of Pharaoh's wife, Jesus, John, the companion of Jurayj, and the companion of the tyrant. He did not mention the Trench; so he left out the companion of the Trench, and with him those who spoke become seven. There is no contradiction between this and his words (peace be upon him), "None spoke in the cradle except three", by way of restriction, for he informed of what was within his knowledge of what had been revealed to him at that time; then after this God, Exalted, taught him what He willed of that, and he informed of it. I say: as for the companion of Joseph, discussion of him will come; as for the companion of Jurayj, the companion of the tyrant and the companion of the Trench, they are in the Ṣaḥīḥ of Muslim. The story of the Trench will come in Sūrat "al-Burūj", God Exalted willing. As for the child of the hairdresser of Pharaoh's wife, al-Bayhaqī mentioned from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "When I was taken on the night journey, I passed through a sweet fragrance and said: What is this fragrance? They said: The hairdresser of Pharaoh's daughter and her children. Her comb fell from her hands and she said: In the name of God. Pharaoh's daughter said: My father? She said: My Lord and your Lord and the Lord of your father. She said: Have you a Lord other than my father? She said: Yes, my Lord and your Lord and the Lord of your father is God. He said: So Pharaoh summoned her and said: Have you a Lord other than me? She said: Yes, my Lord and your Lord is God. He said: So he ordered a hollow vessel of copper, and it was heated, then he ordered that she be cast into it. She said: I have a request of you. He said: What is it? She said: That you gather my bones and the bones of my children in one place. He said: That is yours, because of the right you have over us. So he gave orders concerning them, and they were cast in one after another until it reached a suckling infant among them, who said: Plunge in, O mother, and do not hang back, for we are upon the truth. He said: And four spoke while they were small: this one, the witness of Joseph, the companion of Jurayj, and Jesus son of Mary."

His words, Exalted: She said: My Lord (3:47), that is, O my master. She was addressing Gabriel (peace be upon him), because when he appeared to her in human form he said to her: I am only the messenger of your Lord, to bestow on you a pure boy. When she heard that from his words she enquired about the way the child would come, and said: How shall I have a child when no man has touched me? That is, by marriage. [In her sūrah:] nor have I been unchaste (19:20); she mentioned this for emphasis, because her words "no man has touched me" include the unlawful and the lawful. She is saying: the established custom which God has set in His creation is that a child comes only from marriage or fornication. It was said: she did not deem anything remote from the power of God, Exalted, but she wished to know how this child would come about: from a husband in the future, or would God create him from the first? It is related that Gabriel (peace be upon him), when he said to her "Thus God creates what He wills", He said: Thus said your Lord: It is easy for Me (19:21), blew into the opening of her shift and her sleeve, so said Ibn Jurayj. Ibn ʿAbbās said: Gabriel took the cuff of her shirt with his finger and blew into it, and she conceived Jesus from that hour. Other things have been said, as will be explained in her sūrah, God Exalted willing. Some of them said: Gabriel's breath fell into her womb, and she conceived by that. And some of them said: it is not permissible that the creation be from the breath of Gabriel, because then the child would be partly of the angels and partly of mankind; rather the cause of that is that God, Exalted, when He created Adam and took the covenant from his progeny, placed part of the fluid in the loins of fathers and part of it in the wombs of mothers, and when the two fluids come together they become a child; and God, Exalted, placed both fluids together in Mary, part in her womb and part in her loins, and Gabriel blew into it so that her desire might be stirred, because a woman does not conceive so long as her desire is not stirred; and when her desire was stirred by Gabriel's breath, the fluid that was in her loins fell into her womb, and the two fluids mingled, and she conceived by that. That is His words, Exalted: when He decrees a matter, meaning when He wishes to create a creature, He only says to it: Be, and it is (3:47). The discussion of this has already been given in full in "al-Baqarah".

His words, Exalted: And He will teach him the Book and Wisdom, and the Torah and the Gospel (3:48). Ibn Jurayj said: the Book is writing and script. It was said: it is a book other than the Torah and the Gospel which God taught Jesus (peace be upon him).

and a messenger (3:49), that is, and We shall make him a messenger; or, he shall speak to them as a messenger. It was said: it is conjoined to His words "honoured". Al-Akhfash said: if you wish, you may make the wāw in His words "and a messenger" redundant and "messenger" a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun "him", the implied sense being: and He will teach him the Book as a messenger. In the long ḥadīth of Abū Dharr: "The first of the prophets of the Children of Israel was Moses, and the last of them Jesus (peace be upon him)."
that I create for you, that is, I shape and fashion for you, from clay the likeness of a bird. Al-Aʿraj and Abū Jaʿfar read "ka-hayyah" with doubling; the rest with the hamzah.
"Bird" (al-ṭayr) is treated as both masculine and feminine.

then I breathe into it, that is, into one of them, masculine or feminine, or into the clay, and it becomes a bird (ṭāʾir). Ṭāʾir and ṭayr are like tājir and tajr. Wahb said: it would fly as long as people were looking at it, and when it was out of their sight it fell down dead, so that the act of the creature might be distinguished from the act of God, Exalted. It was said: he created nothing but the bat, because it is the most complete of birds in formation, so that it might be more telling in respect of power, for it has breasts, teeth and ears, and it menstruates and becomes pure and gives birth. It is said: they only asked for the creation of a bat because it is more wonderful than the rest of creation; among its wonders is that it is flesh and blood that flies without feathers, gives birth as animals give birth and does not lay eggs as the rest of birds lay, so that it has an udder from which milk comes; it does not see in the light of day nor in the darkness of night, but only sees at two hours: an hour after the setting of the sun and an hour after the rising of dawn, before it becomes very bright; it laughs as a human laughs, and menstruates as a woman menstruates. It is said that their asking him was by way of obstinacy: they said: Create for us a bat and put a spirit in it, if you are truthful in your claim; so he took clay and made from it a bat, then breathed into it, and lo, it was flying between heaven and earth. The fashioning of the clay and the breathing were from Jesus, and the creation was from God, just as the breathing was from Gabriel and the creation from God. His words, Exalted: and I heal the blind from birth and the leper, and I give life to the dead, by God's leave: the blind from birth (al-akmah) is one who is born blind, according to Ibn ʿAbbās. Abū ʿUbaydah said likewise; he said: he is the one born blind, and he cited Ruʾbah:
> and he turned back as the blind-born turns back.
Ibn Fāris said: al-kamah is blindness with which a person is born, and it may also come upon him later. Suwayd said:
> his eyes went blind until they both turned white.

Mujāhid: he is one who sees by day and does not see by night. ʿIkrimah: he is the weak-sighted; but in the language it is blindness; one says kamiha, yakmahu, kamahan, and kammahtuhā, I, when I blind it (the eye). Leprosy (baraṣ) is well known: it is a whiteness that affects the skin; al-abraṣ is the moon, and sāmm abraṣ (the gecko) is well known, its plural being al-abāriṣ. These two were singled out for mention because they are two incurable diseases. The dominant science in the time of Jesus (peace be upon him) was medicine, so God showed them the miracle in that kind. and I give life to the dead, by God's leave: it was said that he gave life to four persons: al-ʿĀzir{{fn:Lazarus.}}, who was a friend of his; the son of the old woman; the daughter of the tax-collector; and Shem son of Noah; and God knows best. As for al-ʿĀzir, he had died some days before; he called on God, and he rose by God's leave with his fat dripping, and he lived and children were born to him. As for the son of the old woman, he passed by him being carried on his bier; he called on God, and he arose, put on his clothes, carried the bier on his neck and returned to his family. As for the daughter of the tax-collector, a night had passed over her; he called on God, and she lived after that and children were born to her. When they saw that, they said: You give life to one whose death is recent; perhaps they did not die, but a seizure overcame them. So give life for us to Shem son of Noah. He said to them: Show me his grave. He went out, and the people went out with him, until he reached his grave; he called on God, and he came out of his grave with his head gone white. Jesus said to him: How has your head gone white, when there was no greying in your time? He said: O Spirit of God, you called me, and I heard a voice saying: Answer the Spirit of God; and I thought that the Resurrection had come, and from the terror of that my head went white. He asked him about the agony of death, and he said: O Spirit of God, the bitterness of the death-agony has not left my throat; and it had been more than four thousand years since his death. Then he said to the people: Believe him, for he is a prophet. Some of them believed in him, and some of them denied him and said: This is sorcery. It is related from the ḥadīth of Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAyyāsh, who said: Muḥammad ibn Ṭalḥah related to me, from a man, that Jesus son of Mary, when he wished to give life to the dead, would pray two rakʿahs, reciting in the first Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion (67:1) and in the second "Tanzīl al-Sajdah"{{fn:Sūrah 32, al-Sajdah.}}; and when he finished he would praise God and extol Him, then call upon Him by seven names: O Eternal, O Hidden, O Everlasting, O Single, O Odd, O One, O Eternal Refuge. Al-Bayhaqī mentioned it and said: its chain of transmission is not strong.

His words, Exalted: and I inform you of what you eat and what you store in your houses; surely in that is a sign for you, if you are believers (3:49), that is, of that which you eat and what you store. That is because when he gave life for them to the dead, they asked him for another sign and said: Tell us what we eat in our houses and what we store for the morrow. So he told them, saying: O so-and-so, you ate such and such; and you ate such and such and stored such and such. That is His words "and I inform you", the verse. Mujāhid, al-Zuhrī and al-Sakhtiyānī read "wa-mā tadhkharūn" with the dotted dhāl, without doubling. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and others said: he used to tell the children in the school what they had stored, until their fathers prevented them from sitting with him. Qatādah: he told them what they had eaten from the Table and what they had stored from it in secret.

His words, Exalted: And confirming what was before me of the Torah, and to make lawful to you some of what was forbidden to you; and I have come to you with a sign from your Lord, so fear God and obey me. Surely God is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him; this is a straight path (3:50-51). and confirming is conjoined to His words "and a messenger". It was said: the meaning is, and I have come to you confirming.
what was before me: what was prior to me.
and to make lawful to you: there is an ellipsis in it, that is, and to make lawful to you I have come to you.

some of what was forbidden to you, meaning of foods. It was said: Jesus (peace be upon him) made lawful to them only what had been forbidden to them because of their sins and was not in the Torah, such as eating fats and every animal with claws. It was said: he made lawful to them only things which the rabbis had forbidden them, and which were not forbidden to them in the Torah. Abū ʿUbaydah said: it is possible that "some" has the meaning of "all", and he cited Labīd:
> One who forsakes places when I am not pleased with them, / or else its appointed death binds some souls fast.

This view is an error according to the critical scholars among the people of the language, because "some" and "part" do not have the meaning of "all" in this place, since Jesus (peace and blessings be upon him) made lawful to them only some things of what Moses had forbidden them, such as eating fats and other things, and did not make lawful to them killing, theft or indecency. The proof of this is what is related from Qatādah, who said: Jesus came to them with something gentler than what Moses came with (God bless them both and our Prophet), because Moses came to them with the prohibition of camels and some fats, and Jesus came to them making some of them lawful. Al-Nakhaʿī read "baʿḍa alladhī ḥaruma ʿalaykum", like karuma, that is, became forbidden. "Some" may be put in the sense of "all" when a contextual indication is joined to it pointing to that, as the poet{{fn:Ṭarafah ibn al-ʿAbd, addressing the king ʿAmr ibn Hind, whose kunyah was Abū Mundhir, when he had ordered his killing.}} said:
> Abū Mundhir, you have destroyed; so spare some of us. / Have mercy! Some evil is lighter than some.
He means: some evil is lighter than all of it.
and I have come to you with a sign from your Lord: He used the singular, though they are signs, because they are one kind in indicating his messengership.

His words, Exalted: So when Jesus perceived unbelief from them (3:52), that is, from the Children of Israel. "Perceived" (aḥassa) means he knew and found, so said al-Zajjāj. Abū ʿUbaydah said: the meaning of "aḥassa" is he recognised, and the root of that is finding a thing by the sense (ḥāssah). Perception (iḥsās) is knowledge of a thing; God, Exalted, said: Do you perceive any one of them? (19:98). Al-ḥass is killing; God, Exalted, said: when you were slaying them by His leave (3:152). From this is the ḥadīth concerning locusts: "when the cold kills them."
unbelief from them, that is, unbelief in God. It was said: he heard from them the word of unbelief. Al-Farrāʾ said: they intended to kill him.

he said: Who are my helpers towards God? He sought help against them. Al-Suddī, al-Thawrī and others said: the meaning is "with God", so "towards" (ilā) has the meaning of "with", as in His words, Exalted: and do not consume their property along with your property (4:2), that is, with. And God knows best. Al-Ḥasan said: the meaning is, who are my helpers on the way to God, because he called them to God, Mighty and Majestic. It was said: the meaning is, who will join his help to the help of God, Mighty and Majestic. On these two views "towards" retains its ordinary sense, and this is the good view. His seeking help was so that he might be protected by it from his people and proclaim the call openly, according to al-Ḥasan and Mujāhid. This is God's way with His prophets and His friends. Lot said: Would that I had power against you, or could take refuge in a strong support (11:80), that is, a clan and companions who would help me. The disciples said: We are the helpers of God, that is, the helpers of His prophet and His religion. The disciples (ḥawāriyyūn) are the companions of Jesus (peace be upon him), and they were twelve men, so said al-Kalbī and Abū Rawq. There is disagreement as to why they were named thus. Ibn ʿAbbās said: they were named thus for the whiteness of their garments, and they were fishermen. Ibn Abī Najīḥ and Ibn Arṭāh: they were fullers, and were named thus because they whitened garments. ʿAṭāʾ said: Mary handed Jesus over to various trades, and the last to whom she gave him was the disciples, who were fullers and dyers. The master of Jesus wished to travel, and he said to Jesus: I have many garments of different colours, and I have taught you dyeing, so dye them. So Jesus heated a single vat and put all the garments into it, and said: Be, by God's leave, as I wish of you. The disciple came back while all the garments were in the vat, and when he saw them he said: You have ruined them. Then Jesus drew out a red garment, a yellow one and a green one, and so on, each garment in the dye that had been written upon it; the disciple marvelled and knew that this was from God, and he called the people to him and they believed in him; these are the disciples. Qatādah and al-Ḍaḥḥāk: they were named thus because they were the elect of the prophets; the two of them mean because of the purity of their hearts. It was said: they were kings; that is because the king prepared food and invited the people to it, and Jesus was at a bowl which did not diminish; the king said to him: Who are you? He said: Jesus son of Mary. He said: I shall leave this kingdom of mine and follow you. So he went off with those who followed him along with him, and these are the disciples; so said Ibn ʿAwn. The root of ḥawar in the language is whiteness: ḥawwartu al-thiyāb, I whitened the garments; al-ḥuwwārā of food is what has been whitened, that is, bleached; iḥwarra, it became white; and the whitened bowl (al-jafnah al-muḥawwarah) is the one whitened with hump-fat. Al-ḥawārī is also the helper; the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Every prophet has a disciple (ḥawārī), and my disciple is al-Zubayr." Al-ḥawāriyyāt are women, for their whiteness. The poet said:
> So tell the fair women to weep for other than us, / and let none weep for us but the barking dogs.
His words, Exalted: Our Lord, we believe in what You have sent down (3:53), that is, they say: Our Lord, we believe.
in what You have sent down, meaning in Your Book and in the judgement of Yours that You have made manifest.
and we follow the Messenger, meaning Jesus.

so write us down among the witnesses, meaning the community of Muḥammad (peace and blessings be upon him); this is from Ibn ʿAbbās. The meaning is: record our names along with their names and make us of their number. And it has been said: the meaning is, write us down among those who have borne witness to Your prophets that they spoke the truth.

His words, Exalted: And they schemed (3:54), meaning the unbelievers among the Children of Israel, those from whom he perceived unbelief; that is, they schemed to kill him. This was because when Jesus (peace be upon him) had been driven out from among them by his people, he and his mother, he came back to them with the disciples and cried out among them with the call to God, whereupon they resolved to kill him and conspired to assassinate him; that was their scheming. And God's scheming is His leading His servants on step by step (istidrāj) from where they do not know; this is from al-Farrāʾ and others. Ibn ʿAbbās said: Whenever they committed a fresh sin, We renewed for them a favour. Al-Zajjāj said: God's scheming is His requiting them for their scheming, so the requital is named by the name of the initial act, as in His words: God mocks them (2:15) and and He is deceiving them (4:142). This has already been discussed in al-Baqarah. The root meaning of makr (scheming) in the language is contrivance and deception. Makr is also the plumpness of the shank (khadālat al-sāq); one says of a woman that she is mamkūrat al-sāqayn, plump-shanked. And makr is a kind of garment; and it is said, rather it is red ochre (maghrah); Ibn Fāris related this. And it has been said that "God schemed" means His casting the likeness of Jesus upon someone else and raising Jesus to Himself. This was because when the Jews gathered to kill Jesus he entered the house fleeing from them, and Gabriel raised him through the skylight to heaven. Their king then said to a wicked man among them called Judas: Go in to him and kill him. So he went in through the small door and did not find Jesus there, and God cast upon him the likeness of Jesus. When he came out they saw him in the likeness of Jesus, so they seized him, killed him and crucified him. Then they said: His face resembles the face of Jesus, but his body resembles the body of our companion; if this is our companion, then where is Jesus? And if this is Jesus, then where is our companion? Fighting then broke out among them and they killed one another. That is His words, Exalted: And they schemed, and God schemed (3:54). Other explanations than this have been given, as will come.

and God is the best of schemers: an active participle from makara, yamkuru, makran. Some scholars have counted it among the names of God, Exalted, and so one of them says when he supplicates with it: O best of schemers, scheme for me. And he (peace be upon him) used to say in his supplication: "O God, scheme for me and do not scheme against me." We have discussed it in al-Kitāb al-Asnā fī sharḥ asmāʾ Allāh al-ḥusnā. And God knows best.

His words, Exalted: When God said: O Jesus, I am taking you (3:55). The governing word of when is "they schemed", or else an implied verb. A group of the scholars of meanings, among them al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Farrāʾ, said of His words, Exalted, I am taking you and raising you to Myself, that they are by way of anticipation and postponement (taqdīm wa-taʾkhīr), because the conjunction wāw does not impose sequence. The meaning is: I am raising you to Myself and purifying you from those who disbelieve, and taking you after you come down from heaven; as in His words: And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord, it would have been binding, and an appointed term (20:129), the sense being: had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord and an appointed term, it would have been binding. The poet said:
> O palm-tree of Dhāt ʿIrq,
> upon you be, and the mercy of God, peace,

that is, upon you be peace and the mercy of God. Al-Ḥasan and Ibn Jurayj said: the meaning of taking you (mutawaffīka) is seizing you and raising you to heaven without death, like the expression "I took in full (tawaffaytu) my money from so-and-so", that is, I received it. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: God caused Jesus (peace be upon him) to die for three hours of the day, then raised him to heaven. There is something far-fetched in this, for it has been authentically established in the reports from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) that he will descend and kill the Antichrist (al-Dajjāl), as we have set out in the book al-Tadhkirah, and in this book in accordance with what has gone before and what will come. Ibn Zayd said: taking you means seizing you; "taking you" and "raising you" are one and the same, and he has not died yet. Ibn Ṭalḥah related from Ibn ʿAbbās that the meaning of taking you is causing you to die. Al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas: it is the taking of sleep; God, Exalted, said: And it is He who takes you by night (6:60), that is, causes you to sleep, because sleep is the brother of death, as he (peace and blessings be upon him) said when he was asked: Is there sleep in Paradise? He said: "No; sleep is the brother of death, and there is no death in Paradise." Al-Dāraquṭnī transmitted it. The correct view is that God, Exalted, raised him to heaven without death and without sleep, as al-Ḥasan and Ibn Zayd said; this is the preference of al-Ṭabarī, it is what is authentically reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said it. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: The story was that when they wanted to kill Jesus, the disciples gathered in an upper room, twelve men, and the Messiah came in to them through the niche of the room. Iblīs informed the host of the Jews, and four thousand men of them rode out and took hold of the door of the room. The Messiah said to the disciples: Which of you will go out and be killed and be with me in Paradise? A man said: I, O Prophet of God. So he threw over him a tunic (midraʿah) of wool and a turban of wool and handed him his staff, and the likeness of Jesus was cast upon him; he went out to the Jews and they killed him and crucified him. As for the Messiah, God clothed him in feathers and dressed him in light and cut off from him the pleasure of food and drink, and he flew off with the angels. Abū Bakr ibn Abī Shaybah mentioned: Abū Muʿāwiyah related to us: al-Aʿmash related to us, from al-Minhāl, from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: When God, Blessed and Exalted, wished to raise Jesus to heaven, he came out to his companions, who were twelve men, from a spring in the house, his head dripping with water, and said to them: Truly, there is among you one who will disbelieve in me twelve times after having believed in me. Then he said: Which of you will have my likeness cast upon him, and be killed in my place, and be with me in my rank? A young man, one of the youngest of them, stood up and said: I. Jesus said: Sit down. Then he repeated it to them, and the young man stood up and said: I. Jesus said: Sit down. Then he repeated it to them, and the young man stood up and said: I. He said: Yes, you are the one. So God cast upon him the likeness of Jesus (peace be upon him). He said: And God, Exalted, raised Jesus through a skylight (rawzanah) that was in the house up to heaven. He said: And the search party of the Jews came and seized the look-alike and killed him, then crucified him; and some of them disbelieved in him twelve times after having believed in him. They then split into three sects. One sect said: God was among us as long as He willed, then ascended to heaven; these are the Jacobites. Another sect said: The son of God was among us as long as God willed, then God raised him to Himself; these are the Nestorians. And another sect said: The servant of God and His messenger was among us as long as God willed, then He raised him to Himself; these are the Muslims. The two unbelieving sects joined forces against the Muslim one and killed its members, and Islam remained effaced until God sent Muḥammad (peace and blessings be upon him), and then they fought{{fn:The printed text reads "fa-qatalū" (then they killed); the sense is that the believers prevailed, as the verse that follows explains.}}; and God, Exalted, sent down: So a party of the Children of Israel believed and a party disbelieved, and We supported those who believed (61:14), that is, whose fathers had believed in the time of Jesus, against their enemy, by making their religion prevail over the religion of the unbelievers, and they became dominant. In the Ṣaḥīḥ of Muslim, from Abū Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "By God, the son of Mary will surely descend as a just judge; he will surely break the cross, kill the swine and abolish the poll-tax; the young she-camels will surely be left so that no one strives after them; rancour, mutual hatred and mutual envy will surely vanish; and he will surely call people to wealth and no one will accept it." And from him also, from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), who said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, the son of Mary will surely raise the pilgrim's cry (talbiyah) at Fajj al-Rawḥāʾ{{fn:A pass on the road between Mecca and Medina.}}, as a pilgrim or as one performing the lesser pilgrimage, or combining the two." He will not descend with a new law by which he abrogates our law; rather he will descend as a renewer of what has fallen into disuse of it, and as a follower of it, as in the Ṣaḥīḥ of Muslim, from Abū Hurayrah, that the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "How will you be when the son of Mary descends among you and your leader (imām) is from among you?" And in one transmission: "and he leads you from among you" (fa-ammakum minkum). Ibn Abī Dhiʾb said: Do you know what "he leads you from among you" means? I said: Tell me. He said: He leads you by the Book of your Lord, Blessed and Exalted, and the practice (sunnah) of your Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him). We have given this subject fuller exposition in the book al-Tadhkirah, and praise belongs to God. Taking you (mutawaffīka) is originally mutawaffiyuka; the ḍammah was dropped because it was found heavy. It is the predicate of inna. And raising you is conjoined to it, and likewise purifying you, and likewise and placing those who follow you. It is also permissible to read wa-jāʿilu lladhīna (with the participle governing the following noun directly), and that is the original form. And it has been said that the complete pause (waqf tāmm) is at His words and purifying you from those who disbelieve; al-Naḥḥās said: and that is a fine view. and placing those who follow you, O Muḥammad, above those who disbelieve, that is, by the argument and the establishing of proof. And it has been said: by might and victory. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Muḥammad ibn Abān said: what is meant is the disciples. And God, Exalted, knows best.

His words, Exalted: As for those who disbelieve, I shall punish them with a severe punishment in this world and the Hereafter (3:56), meaning by killing, crucifixion, captivity and the poll-tax (jizyah), and in the Hereafter by the Fire.

This We recite to you (3:58): This is in the position of the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence, and its predicate is We recite to you. It is also permissible to take it as "the matter is this", with an implied subject.

His words, Exalted: Truly the likeness of Jesus with God is as the likeness of Adam: He created him from dust (3:59). This is a proof of the validity of analogical reasoning (qiyās). The comparison rests on the fact that Jesus was created without a father, like Adam, not on his having been created from dust. A thing may be likened to another thing even if there is a great difference between them, once they share a single attribute; for Adam was created from dust and Jesus was not created from dust, so there is a difference between them in this respect, but the resemblance between them is that He created both of them without a father. And also because the origin of the creation of both was from dust, since Adam was not created from the dust itself; rather, He made the dust into clay, then made it into dried clay, then created him from it. So likewise Jesus: He turned him from one state to another, then made him a human being without a father. This verse was sent down on account of the delegation of Najrān, when they objected to the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) over his saying "Jesus is the servant of God and His word." They said: Show us a servant who was created without a father. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said to them: "Adam, who was his father? Do you marvel at Jesus having no father? Adam (peace be upon him) had neither father nor mother." That is His words, Exalted: And they bring you no comparison, that is, concerning Jesus, but We bring you the truth, concerning Adam, and a better exposition (25:33). It is related that when he (peace be upon him) called them to Islam they said: We were Muslims before you. He said: "You lie. Three things keep you from Islam: your saying that God has taken a son, your eating of swine, and your prostrating to the cross." They said: Who is the father of Jesus? So God, Exalted, sent down: Truly the likeness of Jesus with God is as the likeness of Adam: He created him from dust, up to His words: then let us invoke the curse of God upon the liars (3:61). The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) then summoned them, and they said to one another: If you do it, the valley will blaze up with fire against you. So they said: Will you not offer us anything other than this? He said: "Islam, or the poll-tax, or war." So they agreed to the poll-tax, as will come. The sentence is complete at His word Adam. Then He said: He created him from dust, then said to him, Be, and he is, that is, and he was. The future tense stands in the place of the past when the meaning is understood. Al-Farrāʾ said: The truth is from your Lord (3:60) is in the nominative by an implied "it" (huwa). Abū ʿUbaydah: it is a fresh sentence, and its predicate is in His words from your Lord. And it has been said that it is the agent, that is, the truth has come to you. So be not of those who doubt: the address is to the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) and those intended are his community, because he (peace and blessings be upon him) was not in doubt about the matter of Jesus (peace be upon him).
There are three questions in this verse.

- The first: His words, Exalted: And whoever disputes with you concerning him (3:61), that is, argues and contends with you, O Muḥammad, concerning him, that is, concerning Jesus, after the knowledge that has come to you that he is the servant of God and His messenger. say: Come, that is, draw near. The word taʿālaw was originally coined for one possessing majesty and elevation, then it came in usage to be employed by anyone calling another to approach; further explanation of it will come in al-Anʿām. let us call is in the position of the jussive. our sons: a proof that the sons of daughters are called sons, for the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) came with al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn, Fāṭimah walking behind him and ʿAlī behind her, and he was saying to them: "When I supplicate, say Amen." then let us pray earnestly (nabtahil), that is, let us humble ourselves in supplication; this is from Ibn ʿAbbās. Abū ʿUbaydah and al-Kisāʾī: let us invoke curses upon one another. The root meaning of ibtihāl is exertion in supplication, with cursing or otherwise. Labīd said:
> Among mature men, lords of his people,
> upon whom Time looked, and then strove earnestly (ibtahal),

that is, strove to destroy them. One says bahalahu Llāh, that is, God cursed him; al-bahl is cursing. Al-bahl is also a small quantity of water. Abhaltuhu means I left him alone with his own wishes; and bahaltuhu likewise. Abū ʿUbaydah related: bahalahu Llāh, yubhiluhu, bahlatan, that is, He cursed him. Ibn ʿAbbās said: They were the people of Najrān: al-Sayyid, al-ʿĀqib and Ibn al-Ḥārith, their chiefs. and invoke the curse of God upon the liars.

- The second: This verse is among the signs of the prophethood of Muḥammad (peace and blessings be upon him), because he called them to the mutual invocation of curses (mubāhalah) and they refused it and were content with the poll-tax, after their leader al-ʿĀqib had told them that if they engaged him in the mutual cursing, the valley would blaze up with fire against them, for Muḥammad is a prophet sent by God; "and you well know that he has brought you the decisive word on the matter of Jesus." So they abandoned the mutual cursing and departed to their land on condition that they pay every year a thousand suits of clothing in Ṣafar and a thousand suits in Rajab, and the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) made peace with them on that basis in lieu of Islam.

- The third: Many scholars have said that his words (peace be upon him) concerning al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn when he engaged in the mutual cursing, let us call our sons and your sons, and his words concerning al-Ḥasan, "This son of mine is a lord (sayyid)", are specific to al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn, that they be called the sons of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) to the exclusion of others, because of his words (peace be upon him): "Every bond and lineage is cut off on the Day of Resurrection except my lineage and my bond." For this reason some of the companions of al-Shāfiʿī said concerning one who makes a bequest to the child of so-and-so, when the latter has no child of his own loins but has a son's child and a daughter's child, that the bequest goes to the son's child and not the daughter's child; and this is the view of al-Shāfiʿī. Further explanation of this will come in al-Anʿām and al-Zukhruf, if God, Exalted, wills.

His words, Exalted: Truly this is the true narrative (3:62). The demonstrative in His words Truly this points to the Qur'an and the narratives it contains. They are called qaṣaṣ because the meanings follow one upon another in them; so it is from their saying "so-and-so follows (yaquṣṣu) the track of so-and-so", that is, he follows him.
and there is no god but God: min is redundant, for emphasis, and the meaning is "and there is no god but God". the Mighty, that is, He who is not overcome.
the Wise: the possessor of wisdom. The like of this has already been discussed, and praise belongs to God.
There are three questions in this verse.

- The first: His words, Exalted: Say: O People of the Book (3:64). The address, according to al-Ḥasan, Ibn Zayd and al-Suddī, is to the people of Najrān; and according to Qatādah, Ibn Jurayj and others, to the Jews of Medina, who were addressed in this way because they had set their rabbis, in the obedience they rendered them, in the place of lords. And it has been said: it is to the Jews and the Christians together. In the letter of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) to Heraclius: "In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful. From Muḥammad, the Messenger of God, to Heraclius, the great one of the Romans. Peace be upon whoever follows the guidance. To proceed: I call you with the summons of Islam. Submit, and you will be safe; submit, and God will give you your reward twice over. But if you turn away, then upon you is the sin of the peasants (arīsiyyīn){{fn:Variously explained as the tillers of the soil, the common people or the subjects, whose sin would fall on the ruler who kept them from Islam.}}. O People of the Book, come to a word common between us and you: that we worship none but God", up to His words then say: Bear witness that we are Muslims. This is the wording of Muslim. Al-sawāʾ means justice and fair dealing; Qatādah said this. Zuhayr said:
> Show me a course in which there is no injustice,
> in which fair dealing (al-sawāʾ) makes us equal.

Al-Farrāʾ: In the sense of justice one also says siwan and suwan; when you give the sīn a fatḥah you lengthen the final vowel, and when you give it a kasrah or a ḍammah you shorten it, as in His words, Exalted: a place equidistant (makānan suwan) (20:58). He said: In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh it is "to a word of justice (ʿadl) between us and you". Qaʿnab read kilmah with the lām unvowelled, transferring the vowel of the lām to the kāf, just as one says kibd (for kabid). So the meaning is: respond to what you have been called to, which is the just and upright word in which there is no deviation from the truth; and He has explained it by His words, Exalted: that we worship none but God. So the position of an is the genitive, as a substitute (badal) for a word; or the nominative, by an implied subject, the sense being "it is that we worship none but God"; or else it is explicative (mufassirah) and has no syntactic position. Along with this, both the indicative and the jussive are permissible in we worship and what is conjoined to it. The jussive is on the basis that an is explicative in the sense of "that is" (ay), as He, Mighty and Majestic, said: that: Walk on (ani mshū) (38:6), and lā is then a jussive particle; this is the doctrine of Sībawayh. On this basis it is also permissible for you to put we worship in the indicative, and what follows it is then a predicate. And the indicative is permissible with the meaning "that we do not worship" (with annahu understood), the like of which is that he did not return to them a word, nor had he power to harm or benefit them (20:89). Al-Kisāʾī and al-Farrāʾ said: and that we associate nothing with Him, and that none of us take are in the jussive, on the supposition that there is no an at the beginning of the sentence.

- The second: His words, Exalted: and that none of us take others as lords besides God, that is, that we do not follow him in declaring anything lawful or unlawful except in what God, Exalted, has made lawful. It is the counterpart of His words, Exalted: They have taken their rabbis and their monks as lords besides God (9:31), the meaning of which is that they set them in the place of their Lord in accepting their declaring unlawful and lawful what God had not made unlawful nor made lawful. This shows the falsity of the doctrine of bare juristic preference (istiḥsān) that does not rest on a legal proof. Al-Kiyā al-Ṭabarī said: like the juristic preferences of Abū Ḥanīfah in the quantitative determinations he fixed without clear grounds. It also contains a refutation of the Rāfiḍah, who say that the word of the Imām must be accepted without his disclosing any legal ground, and that he may make lawful what God has made unlawful without setting out any ground from the revealed Law. Arbāb is the plural of rabb. And dūn here has the meaning of "other than".

- The third: His words, Exalted: But if they turn away, that is, turn aside from what they have been called to. then say: Bear witness that we are Muslims, that is, characterised by the religion of Islam, submissive to its rulings, acknowledging the favours and bounties that God has bestowed upon us in that regard, taking no one as a lord, neither Jesus nor Ezra nor the angels, because they are human beings like us, originated as we are originated; nor do we accept anything from the monks when they forbid us what God has not forbidden us, for then we would have taken them as lords. ʿIkrimah said: the meaning of take is "prostrate". It has already been mentioned that prostration (to persons) continued until the time of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), and then the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) forbade Muʿādh when he wished to prostrate, as its explanation has gone before in al-Baqarah. Anas ibn Mālik related, saying: We said: O Messenger of God, should some of us bow to others? He said: "No." We said: Should some of us embrace others? He said: "No, but shake hands." Ibn Mājah transmitted it in his Sunan. Further explanation of this meaning will come in the sūrah of Yūsuf, if God wills; and in al-Wāqiʿah, touching the Qur'an or part of it without ritual purity, if God, Exalted, wills.

His words, Exalted: So for their breaking of their covenant (4:155). for their breaking is in the genitive by the bāʾ, and the mā in fa-bi-mā is redundant, for emphasis, as in His words: So by mercy from God (fa-bi-mā raḥmatin) (3:159), which has already been discussed. The bāʾ is connected to an elided word, the implied sense being: so for their breaking of their covenant We cursed them; this is from Qatādah and others, and it was elided because the hearer knows it. Abū l-Ḥasan ʿAlī ibn Ḥamzah al-Kisāʾī said: it is connected to what precedes it, and the meaning is "so the thunderbolt seized them for their wrongdoing" (4:153), down to His words So for their breaking of their covenant. He said: He thus explained their wrongdoing, on account of which the thunderbolt seized them, by what follows it, namely their breaking of the covenant, their killing of the prophets and all the other things He set out in which they wronged themselves. Al-Ṭabarī and others rejected this, because those whom the thunderbolt seized were in the time of Moses, whereas those who killed the prophets and hurled the calumny against Mary came a long time after Moses; so the thunderbolt did not seize those whom it seized on account of their hurling the calumny against Mary. Al-Mahdawī and others said: this is not a necessary objection, because it is permissible that He report of them while the ones intended are their forefathers, in accordance with what has already been said in al-Baqarah. Al-Zajjāj said: the meaning is "so for their breaking of their covenant We forbade them good things that had been made lawful to them", because this narrative extends to His words So for the wrongdoing of those who became Jews We forbade (4:160). Their breaking of the covenant was that it had been taken upon them to make plain the description of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him). And it has been said: the meaning is "so for their breaking of their covenant and their doing such-and-such and their doing such-and-such, God set a seal upon their hearts". And it has been said: the meaning is "so for their breaking they do not believe except a few", the fāʾ being intrusive. their disbelief is conjoined (to "breaking"), and likewise their killing. What is meant by the signs of God is their scriptures, which they distorted. Ghulf (wrapped) is the plural of ghilāf (a covering, a sheath), that is: our hearts are receptacles for knowledge, so we have no need of any knowledge other than what we have. And it has been said that it is the plural of aghlaf, which is that which is covered with a wrapping, that is: our hearts are in coverings, so we do not understand what you say; this is like His words: Our hearts are in coverings (41:5). This has already been discussed in al-Baqarah. Their purpose in this was to ward off the argument of the messengers. Setting a seal (ṭabʿ) is sealing (khatm), and this has already been discussed in al-Baqarah. for their disbelief, that is, as a recompense to them for their disbelief, as He said: Rather, God has cursed them for their disbelief, so little is it that they believe (2:88), that is, except a little belief, namely in some of the prophets, and that does not benefit them. Then He repeated and for their disbelief (4:156) to report that they disbelieved with one disbelief after another. And it has been said: the meaning is and for their disbelief in the Messiah, this having been elided because what follows indicates it. The governing word of for their disbelief is the same as the governing word of their breaking, because it is conjoined to it, and it is not permissible for the governing word to be set a seal. The great calumny is their accusing her with Joseph the carpenter, who was one of the righteous among them. Calumny (buhtān) is the excessive lie at which one is astounded, and it has already been discussed. And God, Glorified and Exalted, knows best.

His words, Exalted: and their saying: We killed the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary (4:157). Inna is given a kasrah because it begins a sentence after the verb of saying; giving it a fatḥah is a dialectal usage. The derivation of the word "Messiah" has already been discussed in Āl ʿImrān.
the Messenger of God: a substitute (badal), or if you wish, in the sense of "I mean".
And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him: a refutation of their claim.

but it was made to appear so to them, that is, his likeness was cast upon someone else, as has already been discussed in Āl ʿImrān. And it has been said: they did not know him by sight, and they killed the one they killed while in doubt about him, as He, Exalted, said: And truly those who differ concerning him are in doubt about him. The report, it has been said, is about all of them; and it has been said that only their common people differed about him, and that the meaning of their differing is that some of them said he was a god, and some of them that he was the son of God; al-Ḥasan said this. And it has been said that their differing was that their common people said: We have killed Jesus, while those who witnessed his being raised to heaven said: We did not kill him. And it has been said that their differing was that the Nestorians among the Christians said: Jesus was crucified in respect of his humanity, not in respect of his divinity; while the Melkites said: The crucifixion and the killing befell the Messiah in his entirety, his humanity and his divinity. And it has been said that their differing was that they said: If this is our companion, then where is Jesus? And if this is Jesus, then where is our companion? And it has been said that their differing was that the Jews said: We killed him, because Judas, the chief of the Jews, was the one who worked to have him killed; and a party of the Christians said: Rather, it was we who killed him; and another party of them said: Rather, God raised him to heaven while we were looking on at him.

They have no knowledge of it: min is redundant, and the sentence is complete. Then He, Mighty and Majestic, said: except the following of conjecture: a discontinuous exception (istithnāʾ laysa min al-awwal) in the position of the accusative; it may also be in the position of the nominative as a substitute, that is: they have no knowledge of it except the following of conjecture. Sībawayh recited:
> Many a land in which there is no companion
> except the young gazelles and except the white antelopes.

His words, Exalted: And they did not kill him for certain. Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Suddī said: the meaning is that they did not kill their conjecture with certainty, as when you say "I killed it with knowledge" (qataltuhu ʿilman) when you know a thing completely; so the pronoun refers back to the conjecture. Abū ʿUbayd said: Had the meaning been "they did not kill Jesus for certain", He would have said only "and they did not kill him". And it has been said: the meaning is that they did not kill for certain the one who was made to appear to them as Jesus; on this view the pause is at for certain. And it has been said: the meaning is "they did not kill Jesus", with the pause at and they did not kill him, and for certain is the attribute of an elided verbal noun, and in this there are two construals. One is: that is, they said this as a certain saying; or God said this as a certain saying. The other view is that the meaning be "and they did not know it with certain knowledge". Al-Naḥḥās: If you construe the meaning as "rather God raised him to Himself for certain", that is an error, because what comes after bal does not govern what comes before it, owing to its weakness. Ibn al-Anbārī allowed the pause at and they did not kill him on the basis that for certain is in the accusative by an implied verb which is the complement of an oath, its implied sense being: and you have indeed spoken the truth for certain, that is, a certain truth.

Rather, God raised him to Himself (4:158): the beginning of a fresh sentence; that is, to heaven, for God, Exalted, is far exalted above place. The manner of his being raised has already been discussed in Āl ʿImrān.

And God is Mighty, that is, strong in taking vengeance on the Jews, for He gave power over them to Petrus son of Astīsānūs the Roman{{fn:Some manuscripts read "Ṭīṭūs son of Astīnānūs", that is, Titus son of Vespasian, who destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70.}}, who slew them in a great slaughter.
Wise: He decreed upon them the curse and the wrath.

His words, Exalted: And there is none of the People of the Book but will surely believe in him before his death (4:159). Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid and ʿIkrimah said: the meaning is, he will surely believe in the Messiah before his death, that is, the death of the person of the Book; so the first pronoun refers to Jesus and the second to the person of the Book. This is because there is no one of the People of the Book, the Jews and the Christians, but believes in Jesus (peace be upon him) when he sees the angel with his own eyes; but it is a belief that does not benefit, because it is belief at the moment of despair and when one is already in the state of death. The Jew at that moment acknowledges that he is the Messenger of God, and the Christian acknowledges that he was the Messenger of God. It is related that al-Ḥajjāj asked Shahr ibn Ḥawshab about this verse and said: Captives from among the Jews and the Christians are brought before me and I order that their necks be struck, and I look at such a one at that moment and I see no belief from him. Shahr ibn Ḥawshab said to him: When he sees the affair of the Hereafter with his own eyes, he acknowledges that Jesus is the servant of God and His messenger, and so he believes in him, but it does not benefit him. Al-Ḥajjāj said to him: From where did you take this? He said: I took it from Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyyah. Al-Ḥajjāj said to him: You have taken it from a pure spring. It is related of Mujāhid that he said: There is no one of the People of the Book but believes in Jesus before his death. It was said to him: If he drowns, or burns, or a wild beast eats him, does he believe in Jesus? He said: Yes! And it has been said that both pronouns refer to Jesus (peace be upon him), and the meaning is: whoever is alive at the time of his descent on the Day of Resurrection{{fn:That is, near the coming of the Hour.}} will surely believe in him; Qatādah, Ibn Zayd and others said this, and al-Ṭabarī preferred it. Yazīd ibn Zurayʿ related, from a man, from al-Ḥasan, concerning His words, Exalted, And there is none of the People of the Book but will surely believe in him before his death, that he said: before the death of Jesus; by God, he is alive with God now, but when he descends they will all believe in him. The like of this is reported from al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr. And it has been said: will surely believe in him, that is, in Muḥammad (peace be upon him), even though no mention of him has preceded, because these narratives were sent down to him and the object is belief in him; and belief in Jesus includes belief in Muḥammad (blessings and peace be upon him) as well, since it is not permissible to make a distinction between them. And it has been said: will surely believe in him, that is, in God, Exalted, before he dies, though belief at the moment of seeing with one's own eyes does not benefit him. The first two interpretations are the more evident. Al-Zuhrī related, from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, from Abū Hurayrah, from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), that he said: "The son of Mary will surely descend as a just judge; he will surely kill the Antichrist, kill the swine and break the cross, and prostration will be one, to God, the Lord of the worlds." Then Abū Hurayrah said: Recite if you wish: And there is none of the People of the Book but will surely believe in him before his death. Abū Hurayrah said: before the death of Jesus, repeating it three times. The implied construction of the verse according to Sībawayh is: and there is not anyone of the People of the Book but will surely believe in him. The implied construction of the Kufans is: and there is none of the People of the Book except one who will surely believe in him; but there is an ugliness in this, because it involves the elision of the relative pronoun, while the relative clause is part of the relative pronoun, so it is as if part of the noun has been elided.
His words, Exalted: and on the Day of Resurrection he will be a witness against them, that is, to the denial of those who denied him and the affirmation of those who affirmed him.

His words, Exalted: When God said: O Jesus son of Mary, remember My favour upon you (5:110). This belongs to the description of the Day of Resurrection, as though He said: Remember the Day when God will gather the messengers, and when God says to Jesus such-and-such; al-Mahdawī said this. Jesus may be in the position of the nominative, on the basis that son of Mary is a second vocative; and it may be in the position of the accusative, because it is a vocative in the accusative, as the poet said:
> O Ḥakam son of al-Mundhir son of al-Jārūd,

and the nominative is not permissible in the second element when it is in a construct state, except according to al-Ṭuwāl{{fn:Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad al-Ṭuwāl, a Kufan grammarian and pupil of al-Kisāʾī, d. 243/857.}}. As for His words, Exalted, remember My favour upon you: God, Exalted, reminded Jesus of His favour upon him and upon his mother, although he was mindful of them, for two reasons. The first: so that he might recite to the nations the honour with which He had singled them both out and the loftiness of station by which He had distinguished them. The second: so that He might thereby confirm His argument and refute whoever denies Him. Then He began to enumerate His favours and said: when I strengthened you (ayyadtuka), meaning I fortified you; it is derived from ayd, which is strength, and this has already been discussed. Concerning with the Holy Spirit there are two views. The first: that it is the pure spirit by which God singled him out, as has gone before concerning His words and a spirit from Him (4:171). The second: that it is Gabriel (peace be upon him), and this is the more correct, as has already been said in al-Baqarah.

you spoke to people, meaning: and you spoke to people in the cradle as an infant and in maturity as a prophet. What relates to this has already been discussed in Āl ʿImrān, so there is no point in repeating it. I restrained means I warded off and turned away the Children of Israel from you when they resolved to kill you. when you came to them with the clear proofs, that is, the evidences and the miracles, which are those mentioned in the verse.
and those who disbelieved said, meaning those who did not believe in you and denied your prophethood.
This is nothing, that is, the miracles,
but plain sorcery. Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read la-sāḥirun (but a plain sorcerer), that is: this man is nothing but a sorcerer powerful in sorcery.

His words, Exalted: And when I inspired the disciples: Believe in Me and in My messenger (5:111). The discussion of the meanings of this verse has already been given. Inspiration (waḥy) in the speech of the Arabs means prompting (ilhām), and it is of several kinds: inspiration in the sense of the sending of Gabriel to the messengers (peace be upon them); inspiration in the sense of prompting, as in this verse, that is, I prompted them and cast it into their hearts, and of this kind are His words, Exalted: And your Lord inspired the bee (16:68) and And We inspired the mother of Moses (28:7); and inspiration in the sense of making known, in waking and in dream. Abū ʿUbaydah said: awḥaytu is in the sense of "I commanded", and ilā is a connective particle. One says waḥā and awḥā with one meaning; God, Exalted, said: because your Lord inspired it (awḥā lahā) (99:5), and al-ʿAjjāj said:
> He inspired it (waḥā lahā) to settle, and it settled,
that is, He commanded it (the earth) to be still, and it was still. And it has been said: I inspired here is in the sense of "I commanded them". And it has been said: "I made plain to them".

and bear witness that we are Muslims (bi-annanā), in accordance with the original form; and among the Arabs are those who drop one of the two nūns. That is: bear witness, O Lord. And it has been said: O Jesus, that we have submitted to God.

His words, Exalted: When the disciples said: O Jesus son of Mary (5:112), with the syntactic analysis already given. Can your Lord (hal yastaṭīʿu rabbuka): the reading of al-Kisāʾī, ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Mujāhid is hal tastaṭīʿu, with the tāʾ, and rabbaka in the accusative; al-Kisāʾī assimilated the lām of hal into the tāʾ. The rest read with the yāʾ and rabbuka in the nominative, and this reading is more problematic than the first. Al-Suddī said: the meaning is, will your Lord comply with you (yuṭīʿuka) if you ask Him to send down; so yastaṭīʿu is in the sense of yuṭīʿu, just as they said istajāba in the sense of ajāba (he answered), and likewise istaṭāʿa in the sense of aṭāʿa. And it has been said: the meaning is, is your Lord able? This question was at the beginning of their affair, before their knowledge of God, Mighty and Majestic, had become firm; and for this reason Jesus said in reply, at their error and their deeming permissible of God what is not permissible: Fear God, if you are believers, that is, do not doubt the power of God, Exalted. I say: there is room for doubt about this, because the disciples were the sincere intimates of the prophets, their confidants and their helpers, as He said: Who are my helpers towards God? The disciples said: We are the helpers of God (61:14). And he (peace be upon him) said: "Every prophet has a disciple (ḥawārī), and my disciple is al-Zubayr." It is known that the prophets (God's blessings and peace be upon them) came with the knowledge of God, Exalted, of what is necessarily His, what is possible and what is impossible for Him, and with the duty to convey that to their nations; so how could that be hidden from those who were their intimates and were singled out by them, such that they would be ignorant of the power of God, Exalted? Unless it be said that this came from those who were with them, just as some of the ignorant Bedouin said to the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him): Make for us a Dhāt Anwāṭ as they have a Dhāt Anwāṭ{{fn:A tree venerated in the pre-Islamic period, on which the idolaters hung their weapons.}}, and as those of the people of Moses who said it said: Make for us a god as they have gods (7:138), in accordance with the explanation that will come in al-Aʿrāf, if God, Exalted, wills. And it has been said that the people did not doubt the ability of the Maker, Glorified is He, because they were believers, knowers, possessed of knowledge; it is only like your saying to a man, "Can so-and-so come?" when you already know that he can, the meaning being: will he do that, and will he respond to me in that or not? They knew of God's ability, Exalted, to do that and other things with a knowledge of evidence, report and reflection, and they wanted the knowledge of direct witnessing of it as well, just as Abraham (peace and blessings be upon him) said: My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead (2:260), as has gone before; Abraham already had knowledge of that by report and reflection, but he wanted the direct witnessing into which no uncertainty or doubt can enter, because knowledge by reflection and report may be subject to doubt and objections, whereas knowledge by direct witnessing is subject to none of that. For this reason the disciples said and that our hearts be at rest (5:113), just as Abraham said but so that my heart may be at rest (2:260). I say: this is a fine interpretation, and finer than it is that this was the saying of those who were with the disciples, as will be explained. Ibn al-ʿArabī included "the Able" (al-Mustaṭīʿ) among the names of God, Exalted, saying: Neither the Book nor the Sunnah has transmitted it as a name, but it has been transmitted as a verb; and he cited the saying of the disciples Can your Lord. Ibn al-Ḥaṣṣār refuted him on this in his book Sharḥ al-Sunnah, as did others. Ibn al-Ḥaṣṣār said: His words, Glorified is He, reporting of the disciples' saying to Jesus Can your Lord, is not a doubt about His ability; it is only gentleness in asking and courtesy towards God, Exalted, since not every possible thing is one whose occurrence has been foreordained in His knowledge, nor is it so for everyone. The disciples were the elect of those who believed in Jesus; how then could ignorance of God's power, Exalted, over every possible thing be imputed to them? As for the reading with the tāʾ, it has been said that the meaning is: can you ask your Lord? This is the view of ʿĀʾishah and Mujāhid (may God be pleased with them both). ʿĀʾishah (may God be pleased with her) said: The people knew God, Mighty and Majestic, too well to say "Can your Lord?"; she said: but rather "Can you (ask) your Lord?" It is also related of her that she said: The disciples did not doubt that God is able to send down a table, but they said "Can you (ask) your Lord?" And from Muʿādh ibn Jabal, who said: The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) taught us to recite hal tastaṭīʿu rabbaka. Muʿādh said: And I heard the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) many times recite with the tāʾ, hal tasṭīʿu rabbaka. Al-Zajjāj said: the meaning is, can you call forth the compliance of your Lord in what you ask of Him? And it has been said: can you call upon your Lord, or ask Him? The meanings are close, and there must be an elided element, as He said: And ask the town (12:82); on the reading with the yāʾ no elision is needed.

He said: Fear God, that is, be wary of disobeying Him and of asking too much, for you do not know what may befall you upon demanding signs, since God, Mighty and Majestic, does only what is most beneficial for His servants.
if you are believers, that is, if you are believers in Him and in what I have brought, then there have already come to you signs enough to suffice.

His words, Exalted: They said: We wish to eat of it (5:113), in the subjunctive by an; and that our hearts be at rest, and that we may know that you have spoken the truth to us, and that we may be among the witnesses to it is all conjoined to it. By this they explained the reason for their request when they were forbidden it. Concerning their saying eat of it there are two views. The first: that they wished to eat of it because of a need that called for it. This was because whenever Jesus (peace be upon him) went out, five thousand or more would follow him; some of them were his companions, some of them were seeking that he supplicate for them because of a sickness or ailment they had, being chronically ill or blind, and some of them were watching and mocking. One day he went out to a place and they found themselves in a desert with no provisions, and they grew hungry and said to the disciples: Tell Jesus to pray that a table be sent down upon us from heaven. So Simon (Shamʿūn), the chief of the disciples, came to him and informed him that the people were asking that you pray for a table to be sent down upon them from heaven. Jesus said to Simon: Say to them: Fear God, if you are believers. Simon informed the people of this, and they said to him: Say to him: We wish to eat of it, to the end of the verse. The second: eat of it so that we might obtain its blessing, not because of a need that called them to it. Al-Māwardī said: this is the more likely, because had they been in need they would not have been forbidden to ask. Their saying and that our hearts be at rest admits of three views. The first: that they be at rest in the knowledge that God, Exalted, has sent you to us as a prophet. The second: that they be at rest in the knowledge that God, Exalted, has chosen us for our call. The third: that they be at rest in the knowledge that God, Exalted, has granted us what we asked. Al-Māwardī mentioned these. Al-Mahdawī said: that is, that they be at rest in the knowledge that God has accepted our fasting and our works. Al-Thaʿlabī said: that we may be certain of His power and so our hearts become calm. and that we may know that you have spoken the truth to us, that you are the Messenger of God, and that we may be among the witnesses to it, for God, to His oneness, and for you, to your messengership and prophethood. And it has been said: and that we may be among the witnesses to it for you before those who did not see it, when we return to them.

His words, Exalted: Jesus son of Mary said: O God, our Lord (5:114). The original form, according to Sībawayh, is yā Allāh ("O God"), and the two mīms of Allāhumma stand in place of yā. our Lord is a second vocative; Sībawayh allows nothing else, and it cannot be an adjective qualifying the first, because the first has come to resemble the interjections on account of what has been attached to it.

send down to us a table: the table (māʾidah) is the tray-table (khiwān) on which food is set. Quṭrub said: a māʾidah is not a māʾidah until there is food upon it; if there is none, it is called a khiwān. It is an active participle from māda ʿabdahu, "he fed his servant and gave to him", so the table "gives" (tamīdu) what is upon it, that is, it bestows. From this is the verse of Ruʾbah which al-Akhfash recited:
> The heads of the pampered rivals bring their gifts
> to the Commander of the Faithful, the one from whom bounty is sought (al-mumtād),

that is, the one who is asked and from whom gifts are sought. So the table is that which feeds and gives food to those who eat. The food itself is also called a māʾidah by extension, because it is eaten on the table, just as they call rain "sky" (samāʾ). The people of Kufa said: it was called māʾidah because of its moving with what is upon it, from their saying māda al-shayʾ when a thing sways and moves. The poet said:
> Perhaps you will weep when a dove sings,
> swayed by a leaning bough of the thicket.
And another said:
> And the killing of al-Kinānī after him unsettled me,
> so that the open earth all but swayed beneath me.

From this is His word, Exalted: and He cast upon the earth firm mountains lest it sway with you (16:15). Abū ʿUbaydah said: māʾidah is an active participle with the sense of a passive one, like a pleasing life (69:21), meaning "a life that is pleased with", and gushing water (86:6), meaning "water that is gushed forth".

His words, Exalted: that it may be for us a festival: may be (takūnu) is an adjective qualifying "table", not the apodosis of the request. Al-Aʿmash read takun, in the jussive, as the apodosis. The meaning is: the day of its descent will be a festival for the first of us, that is, for the first of our community and its last. It was said that the Table came down to them on a Sunday, in the morning and in the evening, and for that reason they made Sunday a festival. ʿĪd (festival) is the singular of aʿyād; it is pluralised with a yāʾ, although its root letter is wāw, because the yāʾ is fixed in the singular; and it is said that this is to distinguish it from aʿwād, pieces of wood. One says ʿayyadū, meaning they attended the festival; so al-Jawharī said. It was said that its root is from ʿāda yaʿūdu, "to return", so that it is ʿiwd with a wāw, which was changed to a yāʾ because of the kasrah before it, as in mīzān, mīqāt and mīʿād; thus the day of the Fast-breaking and the day of the Sacrifice were called ʿīd because they return every year. Al-Khalīl said: the ʿīd is any day on which people gather, as though they had returned to it. Ibn al-Anbārī said: it was named ʿīd because of the return to merriment and joy; it is the day of gladness for all creatures. Do you not see that on that day prisoners are not pressed for payment nor punished, neither wild beasts nor birds are hunted, and the boys are not sent off to the schools? It was said that it was named ʿīd because every person returns to the measure of his station: do you not see the difference in their clothing, their appearance and their food, so that some of them host and others are hosted, some show mercy and others are shown mercy? And it was said that it was so named because it is a noble day, by comparison with al-ʿĪd, a noble stallion famous among the Arabs, to which they trace lineage, so that one says "ʿĪdiyyah camels". The poet said:
> ʿĪdiyyah camels, for which the dinars were pledged,

and this has already been discussed. Zayd ibn Thābit read li-ūlānā wa-ukhrānā ("for our first ones and our last ones"), in the plural. Ibn ʿAbbās said: the last of the people will eat from it just as the first of them eat from it. and a sign from You means an evidence and a proof.
and provide for us, that is, give to us.
and You are the best of providers, that is, the best of those who give and provide, for You are the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy.

His words, Exalted: God said: I shall send it down to you (5:115). This is a promise from God, Exalted, with which He answered the request of Jesus, just as Jesus's request had been an answer to the disciples; and this entails that He did send it down, for His promise is true. The people then denied and disbelieved after it had come down, and they were transformed into apes and swine. Ibn ʿUmar said: the people most severely punished on the Day of Resurrection will be the hypocrites, those of the people of the Table who disbelieved, and the house of Pharaoh; God, Exalted, said: but whoever of you disbelieves afterwards, I shall punish him with a punishment with which I punish no one else among all beings.

The scholars differed about the Table, whether it came down or not. The position of the majority, and it is the truth, is that it came down, because of His words, Exalted, I shall send it down to you. Mujāhid said: it did not come down; it is only a parable which God, Exalted, struck for His creatures, forbidding them thereby to ask signs of His prophets. It was said: He promised them an answer, but when He said to them but whoever of you disbelieves afterwards, to the end of the verse, they begged to be excused from it, asked God's forgiveness and said: "We do not want this"; so said al-Ḥasan. This view and the one before it are erroneous; the correct position is that it came down.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: Jesus son of Mary said to the Children of Israel: "Fast thirty days, then ask God for whatever you wish and He will give it to you." So they fasted thirty days and said: "O Jesus, had we worked for anyone and completed our work, he would have fed us; we have fasted and gone hungry, so pray to God to send down to us a table from heaven." Then the angels came bearing a table on which were seven loaves and seven fish, and they set it before them, and the last of the people ate from it as the first of them had eaten.

Abū ʿAbd Allāh Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī al-Tirmidhī al-Ḥakīm mentioned in his Nawādir al-uṣūl: ʿUmar ibn Abī ʿUmar related to us: ʿAmmār ibn Hārūn al-Thaqafī related to us, from Zakariyyāʾ ibn Ḥakīm al-Ḥanẓalī, from ʿAlī ibn Zayd ibn Judʿān, from Abū ʿUthmān al-Nahdī, from Salmān al-Fārisī, who said: When the disciples asked Jesus son of Mary (God's blessings and peace be upon him) for the Table, he rose, put off his woollen garments and put on garments of haircloth, that is, a shirt of black haircloth and a black wrap; then he stood, pressed foot to foot, heel to heel and big toe to big toe, placed his right hand upon his left, then bowed his head in humility before God, then let his eyes flow with weeping until the tears ran down upon his beard and began to drip upon his chest. Then he said: O God, our Lord, send down to us a table from heaven, that it may be for us a festival for the first of us and the last of us, and a sign from You; and provide for us, and You are the best of providers. God said: I shall send it down to you, to the end of the verse. Then there came down a round red cloth (sufrah) between two clouds, one cloud above it and one cloud beneath it, while the people looked on at it. Jesus said: "O God, make it a mercy and do not make it a trial; my God, I ask You for wonders, and You give." It alighted before Jesus (peace be upon him), with a napkin covering it, and Jesus fell down prostrate, and the disciples with him, perceiving from it a fragrant scent the like of which they had never perceived before. Jesus said: "Whichever of you is the most devoted in worship of God, the boldest towards God and the most trusting in God, let him uncover this cloth so that we may eat from it, mention the name of God over it and praise God for it." The disciples said: "O Spirit of God, you have the best right to that." So Jesus (God's blessings be upon him) rose, performed a thorough ablution, prayed a fresh prayer and made many supplications, then sat down at the cloth and uncovered it, and behold, upon it was a grilled fish without bones in it, running with fat as fat runs, with every kind of herb arranged around it except the leek, salt and vinegar at its head, and at its tail five loaves: on one of them five pomegranates, on another dates, and on another olives. Al-Thaʿlabī said: on one of them olives, on the second honey, on the third eggs, on the fourth cheese, and on the fifth dried meat.

Word of this reached the Jews, and they came in grief and heartache to look at it, and they saw a marvel. Simon (Shamʿūn), who was the head of the disciples, said: "O Spirit of God, is it of the food of this world or of the food of Paradise?" Jesus (God's blessings be upon him) said: "Have you not yet parted from these questionings? How I fear for you that you will be punished!" Simon said: "By the God of the Children of Israel, I intended no evil by that." They said: "O Spirit of God, if only there were another sign along with this sign!" Jesus (peace be upon him) said: "O fish, come to life by God's leave!" And the fish quivered, fresh, its eyes glistening, and the disciples were terrified. Jesus said: "What is it with you? I see you ask for a thing, and then when you are given it you dislike it. How I fear for you that you will be punished!" And he said: "It has come down from heaven, and what is on it is neither food of this world nor of the food of Paradise; rather it is something God originated by His consummate power: He said to it 'Be', and it was." Then Jesus said: "O fish, return as you were," and it returned grilled as it had been. The disciples said: "O Spirit of God, be the first to eat from it." Jesus said: "God forbid! Only those who requested it and asked for it shall eat from it." But the disciples refused to eat from it, fearing that it might be an exemplary punishment and a trial. When Jesus saw that, he summoned to it the poor, the needy, the sick, the chronically ill, the lepers, the crippled, the blind and those suffering from dropsy, and said: "Eat of the provision of your Lord and the prayer of your prophet, and praise God for it." And he said: "May the enjoyment be yours and the punishment upon others." So they ate until seven thousand three hundred of them went away belching; and every sick person who ate from it was healed, and every poor person who ate from it was made rich until death.
