When the people saw that, they crowded upon it, and there remained no young or old, no elder or youth, no rich or poor, but they came to eat from it, and they pressed one another. When Jesus saw that, he made it come in turns among them: it would come down one day and not come down the next, like the she-camel of Thamūd, which grazed one day and drank the next. So it came down for forty days, descending in the forenoon and remaining until the shade returned to its place. Al-Thaʿlabī said: it would remain set out and eaten from until, when the shade returned, it flew upwards; the people would eat from it, then it would go back to heaven while the people watched its shadow until it disappeared from them. When forty days were complete, God, Exalted, revealed to Jesus (peace be upon him): "O Jesus, make this Table of Mine for the poor, to the exclusion of the rich." The rich disputed about that, showed enmity to the poor, doubted and made the people doubt. So God said: "O Jesus, I hold to My condition." Thirty-three of them awoke as swine eating excrement, seeking it in the rubbish heaps (akbāʾ), and akbāʾ are refuse heaps, the singular being kibā; this after they had been eating fine food and sleeping on soft beds. When the people saw that, they gathered around Jesus weeping, and the swine came and knelt on their knees before Jesus and began to weep, their tears dripping. Jesus recognised them and began to say: "Are you not so-and-so?" and each would nod his head, unable to speak. They remained thus for seven days, and some say four days; then Jesus prayed God to take their souls, and in the morning no one knew where they had gone: had the earth swallowed them, or what had become of them? I say: there is criticism of this ḥadīth, and it is not sound on account of its chain of transmission.

From Ibn ʿAbbās and Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī: the food of the Table was bread and fish. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: they found in the fish the taste of every food; and al-Thaʿlabī mentioned it. ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir and Qatādah said: it was a table that came down from heaven with fruits of the fruits of Paradise upon it. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: God, Exalted, sent it down as barley cakes and fish. Al-Tirmidhī reported in the chapters on exegesis from ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir, who said: The Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "The Table was sent down from heaven as bread and meat, and they were commanded not to be unfaithful and not to store up for the morrow; but they were unfaithful and stored up and put aside for the morrow, and so they were transformed into apes and swine." Abū ʿĪsā said: this ḥadīth has been related by Abū ʿĀṣim and more than one other from Saʿīd ibn Abī ʿArūbah, from Qatādah, from Khilās, from ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir, as a halted report (mawqūf), and we know it as a raised report (marfūʿ) only from the ḥadīth of al-Ḥasan ibn Qazaʿah. Ḥumayd ibn Masʿadah related to us: Sufyān ibn Ḥabīb related to us, from Saʿīd ibn Abī ʿArūbah, the like of it, and he did not raise it; this is more sound than the ḥadīth of al-Ḥasan ibn Qazaʿah, and we know of no basis for the raised ḥadīth.

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: everything was sent down upon the Table except bread and meat. ʿAṭāʾ said: everything came down upon it except fish and meat. Kaʿb said: the Table came down from heaven inverted, the angels flying with it between heaven and earth, with every food upon it except meat. I say: these three views contradict the ḥadīth of al-Tirmidhī, which is preferable to them, because even if it is not sound as a raised report, it is sound as a halted report from a senior Companion; and God knows best. What is certain is that it came down and that there was food upon it that was eaten; and God knows best what precisely it was.

Abū Nuʿaym mentioned from Kaʿb that it came down a second time for certain devout worshippers of the Children of Israel. Kaʿb said: three men from among the devout worshippers of the Children of Israel met together, gathering in a desert land, each man of them possessing one of the names of God, Exalted. One of them said: "Ask of me, and I shall pray to God for you for whatever you wish." They said: "We ask you to pray to God to bring forth for us in this place a gushing spring, green meadows and fine carpets (ʿabqarī)." He said: so he prayed to God, and behold, a gushing spring, green meadows and fine carpets. Then another of them said: "Ask of me, and I shall pray to God for you for whatever you wish." They said: "We ask you to pray to God to feed us something of the fruits of Paradise." So he prayed to God, and there came down to them a ripening date (busrah), and they ate from it; it was not turned over without their eating from it a different kind; then it was taken up. Then another of them said: "Ask of me, and I shall pray to God for you for whatever you wish." They said: "We ask you to pray to God to send down to us the Table which He sent down to Jesus." He said: so he prayed, and it came down, and they satisfied their need from it; then it was taken up. And he mentioned the rest of the report.
### A question

In the ḥadīth of Salmān mentioned above there is a description of the Table: that it was a cloth (sufrah), not a table with legs. The cloth was the table of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) and the tables of the Arabs. Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Tirmidhī al-Ḥakīm reported: Muḥammad ibn Bashshār related to us: Muʿādh ibn Hishām related to us: my father related to me, from Yūnus, from Qatādah, from Anas, who said: The Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) never ate at a tray-table (khiwān), nor from a small dish (sukurrujah), nor was thin bread ever baked for him. He said: I said to Anas: "On what, then, did they eat?" He said: "On the cloths (sufar)." Muḥammad ibn Bashshār said: this Yūnus is Abū al-Furāt al-Iskāf. I say: this is a sound, well-established ḥadīth, on whose transmitters al-Bukhārī and Muslim agree; al-Tirmidhī reported it, saying: Muḥammad ibn Bashshār related to us: Muʿādh ibn Hishām related to us, and he mentioned it, saying of it: good and rare (ḥasan gharīb).

Al-Tirmidhī Abū ʿAbd Allāh said: the tray-table is an innovated thing which the non-Arabs made, and the Arabs were not ones to make use of it; they used to eat on cloths (sufar), the singular being sufrah, which is what is made from skins and has loops that draw together and open out. It was named sufrah from its opening out, because when its loops are loosened it opens out and discloses (asfarat) what is in it; hence it was called sufrah. A journey (safar) is called safar only because the man thereby comes out (isfār) from the houses. As for his words "nor from a small dish (sukurrujah)", it is because these are vessels for condiments, and condiments are for a variety of dishes, and a variety of dishes was not among their characteristics; their food was rather tharīd, bread sopped in broth, with pieces of meat on it. And he used to say: "Tear the meat with your teeth, for it is more appetising and more wholesome."

If it is said: mention of the table (māʾidah) does occur in the ḥadīths, among them the ḥadīth of Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "Had the lizard (ḍabb) been forbidden, it would not have been eaten at the table of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him)", reported by Muslim and others; and from ʿĀʾishah (may God be pleased with her), who said: The Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "The angels invoke blessings upon a man so long as his table remains laid out", reported by the trustworthy authorities. The reply is that it has been said that the māʾidah is anything that is stretched out and spread, such as the napkin and the cloth. Properly, the dāl of its root ought to be doubled, but they made one of the two dāls a yāʾ, and so it was said māʾidah. The action falls upon it, so it ought properly to have been "stretched out" (mamdūdah), in the passive, but it was given in the language the form of the active participle, just as they said "a concealing secret" (sirr kātim) when it is in fact concealed (maktūm), and "a pleasing life" (ʿīshah rāḍiyah) when it is in fact pleased with (marḍiyyah); and likewise in the language what is active was given the form of the passive, as they said "an ill-omened man" (rajul mashʾūm) when he is in fact one who brings ill omen (shāʾim), and "a veiled screen" (ḥijāb mastūr) when it is in fact one that veils (sātir). He said: so the khiwān is what is raised from the ground on its legs; the māʾidah is what is stretched out and spread; and the sufrah is what discloses what is inside it, because it is drawn together by its loops. From al-Ḥasan, who said: eating at a tray-table is the practice of kings, on a napkin the practice of the non-Arabs, and on a cloth the practice of the Arabs, and it is the Sunnah. And God knows best.

His words, Exalted: And when God said: O Jesus son of Mary, did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides God"? (5:116). There is disagreement about the time of this speech. Qatādah, Ibn Jurayj and most of the commentators said: this will be said to him only on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Suddī and Quṭrub said: He said this to him when He raised him to heaven and the Christians said about him what they said; and they argued from His words If You punish them, they are Your servants (5:118), and from the fact that idh ("when") in the speech of the Arabs refers to what is past. The first is the more correct, as is shown by what precedes it, His words on the Day when God will gather the messengers (5:109) to the end of the verse, and by what follows it, This is the Day when the truthful will profit from their truthfulness (5:119). On this view idh has the sense of idhā ("when", of the future), as in His words, Exalted, if you could but see when they are terrified (34:51), that is, when (idhā) they will be terrified. Abū al-Najm said:
> Then may God reward him on my behalf, when (idh) He rewards,
> with Gardens of Eden in the heavens on high,
meaning "when (idhā) He rewards". Al-Aswad ibn Jaʿfar al-Azdī said:
> So now, when (idh) I jest with them, they only
> say: "Behold, the old man has not gone the way he should",

meaning "when (idhā) I jest with them". So the future is expressed with the wording of the past, because it is a matter whose occurrence is certain and whose proof is manifest, as if it had already taken place. In the Revelation there is And the companions of the Fire will call out to the companions of the Garden (7:50), where the verb is in the past tense; there are many instances like this, and it has been discussed before.

The people of interpretation differed as to the meaning of this question, which is not a true interrogative even though it is cast in the form of an interrogative, holding two views. The first: that He asked him this as a rebuke to those who made this claim about him, so that his denial after the question would be more forceful in giving them the lie and more severe in rebuke and reproach. The second: that He intended by this question to inform him that his people had altered things after him and had attributed to him what he never said.

If it is asked: the Christians did not take Mary as a god, so how could this be said about them? The reply is: since it was part of their doctrine that she did not give birth to a human being but gave birth to a god, it necessarily followed for them to say that she, by reason of her partaking in him, was of the same standing as the one whom she bore; and when that consequence bound them, they became of the same standing as those who say it.

His words, Exalted: He said: Glory be to You! It is not for me to say what I have no right to. If I had said it, You would have known it. Al-Tirmidhī reported from Abū Hurayrah, who said: Jesus received his argument, and God instructed him in it, with regard to His words And when God said: O Jesus son of Mary, did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides God"? Abū Hurayrah said, from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him): "So God instructed him: Glory be to You! It is not for me to say what I have no right to", the whole verse. Abū ʿĪsā said: this is a good, sound ḥadīth (ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ).

He began with glorification before the answer for two reasons. The first: to declare Him transcendent above what had been attributed to Him. The second: in submission to His might and in fear of His power. It is said that when God, Exalted, said to Jesus did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides God"?, trembling seized him at that speech until he heard the sound of his own bones within himself, and he said Glory be to You! Then he said It is not for me to say what I have no right to, that is, to claim for myself what is not my due; meaning: I am one who has a Lord, and am not a lord; a worshipper, and not one worshipped. Then he said If I had said it, You would have known it, thus referring the matter to His knowledge; and God already knew that he had not said it, but He asked him about it as a reproach to those who took Jesus as a god. Then he said You know what is in my self, and I do not know what is in Your Self, that is, You know what is hidden in me, and I do not know what is hidden with You. It was said that the meaning is: You know what I know, and I do not know what You know. It was said: You know what I conceal, and I do not know what You conceal. It was said: You know what I intend, and I do not know what You intend. It was said: You know my secret, and I do not know Your secret, because the seat of the secret is the self (nafs). And it was said: You know what proceeded from me in the abode of this world, and I do not know what will proceed from You in the abode of the Hereafter. I say: the meaning in these sayings is close to one another, namely: You know my secret and what my inner conscience, which You created, enfolds, and I know nothing of what You have reserved to Yourself of Your unseen and Your knowledge.
Indeed, You are the Knower of all things unseen: what was, what will be, what has not been, and what is.
His words, Exalted: I said to them nothing except what You commanded me (5:117), meaning in this world, with the profession of God's oneness (tawḥīd).

that: "Worship God": an ("that") has no syntactic position; it is explicative (mufassirah), like and the chiefs among them went off, [saying] that: "Walk on" (38:6). It may also be in the position of an accusative, that is, "I mentioned nothing to them except the worship of God"; and it may be in the position of a genitive, that is, "[commanded me] with: Worship God". Giving the nūn a ḍammah is preferable, because they find a kasrah followed by a ḍammah burdensome, though the kasrah is permissible on the basic principle governing the meeting of two quiescent letters. His words, Exalted: and I was a witness over them, that is, a guardian over them with regard to what You commanded them.
so long as I remained among them: mā is in the accusative position, that is, "during the time of my remaining among them".

but when You took me up, You were the Watcher over them: it has been said that this indicates that God, Mighty and Majestic, caused him to die before raising him; but this is nothing, because the reports have come abundantly that he was raised, that he is alive in heaven, and that he will descend and kill the Antichrist (al-Dajjāl), as will be explained later. The meaning is rather: when You raised me to heaven. Al-Ḥasan said: "being taken" (wafāh) in the Book of God, Mighty and Majestic, bears three senses: the taking of death, as in His words, Exalted, God takes the souls at the time of their death (39:42), meaning at the time of the expiry of their term; the taking of sleep, as God, Exalted, said, It is He who takes you by night (6:60), meaning He who causes you to sleep; and the taking of raising up, as God, Exalted, said, O Jesus, I am taking you up (3:55). His words You were (kunta anta): anta here is for emphasis; the Watcher is the predicate of kunta, and its meaning is the Guardian over them, the Knower of them and the Witness to their deeds. Its root is murāqabah, that is, watchful observation, and from it comes marqabah, the watch-tower, because it is the place of the watchman by reason of the height of the position.

and You are Witness over all things, that is, over my speech and their speech; and it was said: over whoever disobeys and whoever obeys. Muslim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: The Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) stood up among us to preach with an exhortation and said: "O people, you will be gathered to God barefoot, naked and uncircumcised: As We began the first creation, We shall repeat it: a promise binding upon Us; truly We shall do it (21:104). Behold, the first of creatures to be clothed on the Day of Resurrection will be Abraham (peace be upon him). Behold, men from my community will be brought and taken off towards the left, and I shall say: 'My Lord, my companions!' And it will be said: 'You do not know what they innovated after you.' So I shall say as the righteous servant said: and I was a witness over them so long as I remained among them; but when You took me up, You were the Watcher over them, and You are Witness over all things. If You punish them, they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, You are indeed the Mighty, the Wise (5:117–118)." He said: "Then it will be said to me: 'They never ceased turning back, apostates upon their heels, since you parted from them.'"

His words, Exalted: If You punish them, they are Your servants (5:118): a conditional clause with its apodosis; and and if You forgive them, You are indeed the Mighty, the Wise is the same. Al-Nasāʾī related from Abū Dharr, who said: The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) stood one night in prayer with a single verse until morning came, and the verse was If You punish them, they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, You are indeed the Mighty, the Wise.

There is disagreement about its interpretation. It was said: he said it by way of seeking kindness and compassion for them, as a master is entreated on behalf of his slave; and for this reason he did not say "for they have disobeyed You". It was said: he said it by way of submission to His command and seeking refuge from His punishment, while knowing that an unbeliever is not forgiven. It was said: the hāʾ and mīm, the pronoun "them", in If You punish them refer to those of them who died in unbelief, and the hāʾ and mīm in if You forgive them refer to those of them who repented before death; and this is a fine view. As for the view of those who say that Jesus (peace be upon him) did not know that the unbeliever is not forgiven, it is a view that presumes against the Book of God, Mighty and Majestic, because the reports that come from God, Mighty and Majestic, are not abrogated. It was said: Jesus was of the opinion that they had introduced acts of disobedience and had done after him what he had not commanded them, but that they were still upon the pillar of his religion; so he said: and if You forgive them the acts of disobedience that they introduced after me. He said You are indeed the Mighty, the Wise and did not say "You are indeed the Forgiving, the Merciful", in keeping with what the narrative requires of submission to His command and entrusting the matter to His judgement. Had he said "You are indeed the Forgiving, the Merciful", it would have suggested a prayer for forgiveness for one who died in his polytheism, and that is impossible. So the implied sense is: if You leave them in their unbelief until they die and punish them, they are Your servants; and if You guide them to Your oneness and obedience to You and so forgive them, You are indeed the Mighty, whom nothing You will can resist, the Wise in what You do: You lead astray whom You will and guide whom You will. A group did read "You are indeed the Forgiving, the Merciful", but it is not in the written codex (muṣḥaf); al-Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ mentioned it in his book al-Shifāʾ.

Abū Bakr al-Anbārī said: Those who say that His words You are indeed the Mighty, the Wise do not match His words and if You forgive them, because what matches forgiveness is "You are indeed the Forgiving, the Merciful", have attacked the Qurʾān. The answer is that it admits of nothing but what God sent down, and whenever it is transferred to the wording to which this person would transfer it, its meaning is weakened; for "the Forgiving, the Merciful" would then stand alone with the second condition and have no connection with the first condition, whereas according to what God, Mighty and Majestic, sent down, and on whose recitation the Muslims are agreed, it is joined to both conditions, the first and the last, since its summary sense is: "If You punish them, You are indeed Mighty, Wise; and if You forgive them, You are indeed the Mighty, the Wise", in both matters, punishment and forgiveness. So "the Mighty, the Wise" was more fitting for this place because of its generality, since it embraces both conditions, and "the Forgiving, the Merciful" was not suitable, since it does not admit of the generality that "the Mighty, the Wise" admits of; and what bears witness to the magnifying of God, Exalted, to His justice and to praise of Him throughout the whole verse and both the conditions mentioned is more fitting, and firmer in meaning within the verse, than what suits one part of the speech and not another.

Muslim reported, by more than one route, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) recited His words, Mighty and Majestic, concerning Abraham, My Lord, they have led astray many of mankind; so whoever follows me is of me, and whoever disobeys me, You are indeed Forgiving, Merciful (14:36), and what Jesus (peace be upon him) said, If You punish them, they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, You are indeed the Mighty, the Wise; then he raised his hands and said: "O God, my community!" and wept. So God, Mighty and Majestic, said: "O Gabriel, go to Muḥammad (and your Lord knows best) and ask him what makes him weep." Gabriel (peace be upon him) came to him and asked him, and the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) told him what he had said, and He knows best. Then God said: "O Gabriel, go to Muḥammad and say to him: We shall satisfy you regarding your community and We shall not grieve you."

Some said: there is a transposition (taqdīm wa-taʾkhīr) in the verse, and its meaning is: if You punish them, You are indeed the Mighty, the Wise; and if You forgive them, they are Your servants. But taking the words in their order is preferable, for the reason we have explained. And with God is success.

His words, Exalted: God said: This is the Day when the truthful will profit from their truthfulness (5:119), that is, their truthfulness in this world; as for the Hereafter, truthfulness there is of no avail. Their truthfulness in this world may mean their sincerity in acting for God, or it may mean their refraining from lying against Him and against His messengers. Truthfulness profits them on that Day, even though it is beneficial on every day, because recompense takes place on it. It was said: what is meant is their truthfulness in the Hereafter, namely in testifying for their prophets that they conveyed the message, and in what they testify against themselves concerning their deeds; and the manner of its profiting them would be that they are spared being called to account, because they did not conceal testimony, so that they are forgiven for their acknowledgement in favour of their prophets and against themselves. And God knows best.

Nāfiʿ and Ibn Muḥayṣin read yawma ("Day") in the accusative. The rest read it in the nominative, and this is the clear reading, on the basis of subject and predicate: yawmu yanfaʿu ("the Day when ... will profit") is the predicate of "this", and the sentence is in the accusative position as the object of "said". As for the reading of Nāfiʿ and Ibn Muḥayṣin, Ibrāhīm ibn Ḥumayd related from Muḥammad ibn Yazīd that this reading is not permissible, because it would be putting the predicate of the subject in the accusative, and indeclinability is not permissible in it. Ibrāhīm ibn al-Sarī said: it is permissible, in the sense "God said this to Jesus son of Mary on the Day when the truthful profit from their truthfulness", so that "Day" is an adverb of the saying and "this" is the object of the saying, the implied sense being: God said this saying on a Day when the truthful profit. It was said: the implied sense is, God, Mighty and Majestic, said: these things profit on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Kisāʾī and al-Farrāʾ said: yawm is here made indeclinable with a fatḥah because it is annexed to something other than a noun, as you say maḍā yawmaʾidhin ("that day passed"); and al-Kisāʾī recited:
> At the time when I reproached grey hair for youthful folly,
> and said: "Have I not yet sobered, with grey hair to restrain me?"

Al-Zajjāj said: the Basrans do not allow what these two said when you annex the adverb to an imperfect verb; if it is to a past verb, it is good, as in the preceding verse of poetry. It is permissible to annex a verb to adverbs of time only because the verb has the sense of a verbal noun. It was said: it may be in the accusative as an adverb and still be the predicate of the subject "this", because the latter points to an event, and adverbs of time serve as predicates of events: you say "the fighting is today" and "the departure is this hour"; and the sentence is in the accusative position as the object of "said". It was said: it may be that "this" is in the nominative position as subject, and "Day" is the predicate of the subject, with the governing word elided, the implied sense being: God said: this which We have related will take place on the Day when the truthful profit from their truthfulness. There is a third reading, yawmun yanfaʿu with tanwīn, "a Day [on which] the truthful [profit] from their truthfulness", with an ellipsis in the speech whose implied sense is "on it", like His words and fear a Day on which no soul shall avail another soul at all (2:48); this is the reading of al-Aʿmash.

His words, Exalted: For them are Gardens: subject and predicate. flowing is in the position of an adjective. beneath which, that is, beneath its chambers and its trees, as has been explained before. Then He, Exalted, made clear their reward and that He is pleased with them, with a pleasure after which He will never be angry; and they are pleased with Him, that is, with the recompense with which He has rewarded them.
That is the triumph, that is, the victory; supreme, that is, that whose good is great and abundant, and whose possessor's station is raised high and ennobled.

His words, Exalted: To God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth (5:120), to the end of the verse. This came after what had passed of the Christians' claim about Jesus, that he is a god; so He, Exalted, declared that the dominion of the heavens and the earth belongs to Him, to the exclusion of Jesus and of all other created beings. The meaning may also be that He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth gives the Gardens mentioned above to the obedient among His servants; may God make us among them by His favour and His generosity. The Sūrah of the Table is completed, with praise to God, Exalted.

His words, Exalted: And mention in the Book Mary (19:16), that is, her story to its end. This is the beginning of a story which is not part of the preceding one. The address is to Muḥammad (peace and blessings be upon him), that is: make her story known to them so that they may know the perfection of Our power.
when she withdrew (19:16), that is, she went aside and drew apart. Nabdh is casting and throwing; God, Exalted, said: but they cast it behind their backs (3:187).

from her people (19:16), that is, from those who were with her. "When" (idh) stands in apposition (badal) to "Mary", an apposition of inclusion (badal ishtimāl), because times include whatever takes place in them. Withdrawal (intibādh) is seclusion and being alone. People differed as to why she withdrew. Al-Suddī said: she withdrew to purify herself from menstruation or post-natal bleeding. Others said: to worship God, and this is good. That is because Mary (peace be upon her) was dedicated to the custody of the sanctuary, to its service and to worship in it, so she went aside from the people for that purpose and entered the sanctuary beside the prayer-niche (miḥrāb), on its eastern side, to be alone for worship, and Gabriel (peace be upon him) came in to her. So His words an eastern place (19:16) mean a place on the eastern side. Al-sharq, with the rāʾ unvowelled, is the place in which the sun rises, and al-sharaq, with the rāʾ vowelled with a, is the sun. The place was specified as eastern only because they used to venerate the direction of the east, from where the lights rise, and the eastern side of everything was more excellent, in their eyes, than any other; al-Ṭabarī related this. It is related of Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: I am the most knowledgeable of people as to why the Christians took the east as their direction of prayer (qiblah): it is because of the words of God, Mighty and Majestic, when she withdrew from her people to an eastern place; so they took the birthplace of Jesus (peace be upon him) as a direction of prayer, and they said: had any part of the earth been better than the east, Mary would have given birth to Jesus (peace be upon him) there. People differed about the prophethood of Mary. It was said: she was a prophetess, by virtue of this sending and her conversing with the angel. And it was said: she was not a prophetess; rather what spoke to her was something in the likeness of a human being, and her seeing the angel was like Gabriel (peace be upon him) being seen in the form of Diḥyah al-Kalbī when he asked about faith and Islam. The first is the more evident. The discussion of this matter has already been given in full in Āl ʿImrān, and praise be to God.

His words, Exalted: then We sent to her Our Spirit (19:17). It was said: it is the spirit of Jesus (peace be upon him), because God, Exalted, created the spirits before the bodies, and He placed the spirit in the body of Jesus (peace be upon him) which He created in her womb. And it was said: it is Gabriel, and the spirit was ascribed to God, Exalted, by way of distinction and honour. The evident meaning is that it is Gabriel (peace be upon him), because of His words and he appeared to her (19:17), that is, the angel took on a form before her.
as a human being (19:17): an explanatory term, or a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl).

well-proportioned (19:17), that is, of even constitution, because she could not have borne, or looked upon, Gabriel in his own form. When she saw a man of handsome appearance, in human form, who had broken through the veil upon her, she thought that he meant her harm, so she said: I take refuge in the All-Merciful from you, if you are God-fearing (19:18), that is, one of those who fear God. Al-Bikālī said: Gabriel (peace be upon him) recoiled in alarm at the mention of the All-Merciful, Blessed and Exalted. Al-Thaʿlabī said: he was a righteous man, so she sought refuge against him out of astonishment. And it was said: taqī is of the pattern faʿīl in the sense of mafʿūl, that is: if you were one against whom refuge is sought. In al-Bukhārī, Abū Wāʾil said: Mary knew that the God-fearing man is possessed of restraint when she said if you are God-fearing. And it was said: Taqī was the name of a notorious profligate of that time; Wahb ibn Munabbih said this, and Makkī and others related it. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: it is weak and goes along with mere conjecture. Then Gabriel (peace be upon him) said to her: I am only a messenger of your Lord, to give you a pure boy (19:19).

He made the gift come from himself, since the announcement of it came from him. Warsh, from Nāfiʿ, read "li-yahaba laki" ("that He may give you"), in the sense of: God sent me that He might give you. And it was said: the meaning of "li-ahaba" with the hamzah is construed according to the sense, that is, He said: I sent him that I might give you. And "li-yahaba" without hamzah may possibly be in the sense of the form with hamzah, the hamzah having then been lightened. When Mary heard this from him she asked about the manner of it, and she said: how shall I have a boy when no man has touched me (19:20), that is, by marriage.

nor have I been unchaste (19:20), that is, a fornicatress. She mentioned this for emphasis, because her words "no man has touched me" cover both the lawful and the unlawful. And it was said: she did not consider anything beyond the power of God, Exalted, but she wished to know how this child would come about: through a husband in the future, or would God create him directly? It is related that Gabriel (peace be upon him), when he said these words to her, blew into the opening of her garment and her sleeve; Ibn Jurayj said this. Ibn ʿAbbās said: Gabriel (peace be upon him) took the sleeve of her shift with his finger and blew into it, and she conceived Jesus that very hour. Al-Ṭabarī said: the Christians claimed that Mary conceived Jesus when she was thirteen years old, that Jesus lived until he was raised up thirty-two years and some days, and that Mary remained six years after his being raised, so that her whole lifetime was fifty-odd years. His words and that We may make him (19:21) are connected to an elided verb, that is: and We create him so that We may make him a sign, a wondrous proof of Our power, and a mercy, that is, for whoever believes in him.
and it was a matter decreed (19:21): predetermined, written on the Tablet.

His words, Exalted: So she conceived him, and withdrew with him to a distant place (19:22), that is, she went aside with the pregnancy to a far-off place. Ibn ʿAbbās said: to the farthest end of the valley, which is the valley of Bethlehem, between which and Aelia{{fn:Īliyāʾ, Aelia, the old name of Jerusalem.}} there are four miles. She went far off only to flee from her people's reproaching her for giving birth without a husband. Ibn ʿAbbās said: no sooner had she conceived than she gave birth at once; and this is the evident meaning, because God, Exalted, mentioned the withdrawal immediately after the conception. And other things were said, as will come. His words, Exalted: then the pangs of childbirth drove her to the trunk of the palm tree (19:23). "Ajāʾahā" means "compelled her"; it is the verb jāʾa made transitive by the hamzah. One says jāʾa bihi and ajāʾahu to such-and-such a place, just as one says dhahaba bihi and adhhabahu. Shubayl read, and it is also related from ʿĀṣim, "fājaʾahā" ("came upon her suddenly"), from mufājaʾah. In the codex of Ubayy: "and when the pangs of childbirth drove her". Zuhayr said:
> And many a protected neighbour journeyed purposefully to us, driven to us by fear and by hope.

The majority read "al-makhāḍ" with a on the mīm, and Ibn Kathīr, in what is related from him, with i; it is the labour pains, the severity of childbirth and its pangs. One says makhiḍat al-marʾatu tamkhaḍu makhāḍan and mikhāḍan; and nāqatun mākhiḍ means a she-camel whose time of giving birth has drawn near. to the trunk of the palm tree: it is as though she sought something to lean upon and cling to, as a woman in labour clings because of the severity of the pains of childbirth. The trunk (jidhʿ) is the stem of the dried palm in the desert which has neither fronds nor branch upon it, and for this reason He did not say "to the palm tree".

She said: would that I had died before this (19:23). Mary (peace be upon her) wished for death for reasons of religion, on two counts. The first: she feared that evil would be thought of her in her religion and that she would be reproached, and that this would be a trial to her. The second: lest a people should fall, on her account, into slander and the imputation of fornication, and that is destructive. Within this limit the wishing for death is permissible, and this matter has already been explained in the sūrah of Joseph (peace be upon him), and praise be to God. I say: I have heard that Mary (peace be upon her) heard the call of one who said: "Come forth, O you who shall be worshipped apart from God!" and she grieved at that and said: would that I had died before this and been a thing forgotten, consigned to oblivion (19:23). Nisy in the speech of the Arabs is the paltry thing whose nature it is to be forgotten and whose loss causes no pain, like a tent-peg or a rope for the traveller, and the like.

It is related of the Arabs that when they wanted to depart from a camping place they would say: "Look to your ansāʾ"; ansāʾ is the plural of nisy, which is the paltry thing that is overlooked and so forgotten. From this is the saying of al-Kumayt (may God, Exalted, be pleased with him):
> Do you make us a bridge for Kalb of Quḍāʿah, when I am no forgotten trifle among Maʿadd, nor an interloper?

Al-Farrāʾ said: nisy is what a woman casts away of the rags of her monthly indisposition, so Mary's words "nasyan mansiyyan" mean a discarded menstrual cloth. It was also read "nasyan" with a on the nūn, and the two are dialectal variants like ḥijr and ḥajar, witr and watr. Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī read with hamzah, "nisʾan", with i on the nūn. Nawf al-Bikālī read "nasʾan" with a on the nūn, from nasaʾa Allāhu fī ajalihi, that is, He deferred his term. Abū al-Fatḥ and al-Dānī related this from Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb. Bakr ibn Ḥabīb read "nassan" with the sīn doubled and a on the nūn, without hamzah. Al-Ṭabarī related among her stories that when she conceived Jesus (peace be upon him) her sister also conceived John, and her sister came to visit her and said: "Mary, have you perceived that I am with child?" And she said to her: "And I find that what is in my womb bows down to what is in your womb." That is because it is related that she felt her unborn child bowing with its head towards the side of Mary's womb. Al-Suddī said: that is His word: confirming a word from God, and a chief, and chaste, and a prophet from among the righteous (3:39). It is also mentioned among her stories that she went out in flight with a man of the Children of Israel called Joseph the carpenter, who used to serve with her in the sanctuary, and the narrator went on at length about this. Al-Kalbī said: Joseph was told, it having been given out to him that she had conceived by fornication: "Now the king will kill her", so he fled with her; and on the road he was minded to kill her, but Gabriel (peace be upon him) came to him and said to him: "He is from the Holy Spirit." Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: all of this is weak. This story requires that she conceived and continued pregnant in the customary way of women, and the reports concur that she gave birth to him after eight months; ʿIkrimah said this, and for this reason it is said that no eight-months' child lives, to preserve the special distinction of Jesus. And it was said: she bore him after nine; and it was said: after six. And what we have mentioned from Ibn ʿAbbās is the soundest and most evident. And God knows best.

His words, Exalted: Then he called to her from beneath her (19:24). It was read with a on the mīm and with i.{{fn:That is, man taḥtahā, "he who was beneath her", and min taḥtihā, "from beneath her".}} Ibn ʿAbbās said: what is meant by "man" is Gabriel, and Jesus did not speak until she brought him to her people; ʿAlqamah, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Qatādah said this too. In this there was for her a sign and a token that this was one of those matters that break the ordinary course of things, in which God, Exalted, has a mighty purpose. His words do not grieve (19:24) are the explanation of the call, and "an" is explicative, in the sense of "that is"; the meaning is: so do not grieve over your giving birth.

Your Lord has placed beneath you a sarī (19:24), meaning Jesus. The sarī among men is the one great in qualities, the chief. Al-Ḥasan said: by God, he was a sarī among men. One says sariya fulānun ʿalā fulānin, meaning he showed himself generous towards him; and so-and-so is a sarī from a people who are sarāh. The majority said: he pointed her to the stream which was near the trunk of the palm tree. Ibn ʿAbbās said: it was a river whose water had ceased to flow, and God, Exalted, made it flow for Mary. The river is called sarī because the water runs (yasrī) in it. The poet said:

> A one-handled bucket, from which you see the drawer of water bent askew; when it gulps in the stream, it gurgles.{{fn:Salm: a bucket with a single handle, like a water-carrier's; al-dālī: the one who draws water with the bucket; harhara: the sound of running water.}}
And Labīd said:

> So the two of them waded into the midst of the stream and cleft a brimming pool whose rushes grew close together.{{fn:From his Muʿallaqah; the two are the wild ass and his mate, parting the plants that grow upon the water.}}

And it was said: it was Jesus who called to her, and that was a miracle and a sign and a comfort to her heart; but the first is the more evident. Ibn ʿAbbās read: "then an angel called to her from beneath her". They said: Gabriel (peace be upon him) was on a spot of ground lower than the spot on which she was.
His words, Exalted: And shake towards you the trunk of the palm tree; it will drop upon you fresh ripe dates. So eat and drink and be comforted (19:25-26). In this there are four questions:

- The first: His words, Exalted, and shake. He commanded her to shake the dry trunk so that she might see another sign in the quickening of the dead trunk. The bāʾ in His words "bi-jidhʿ" is redundant, for emphasis, as one says khudh bi-l-zimām ("take hold of the rein") and aʿṭi bi-yadika ("give with your hand"). God, Exalted, said: let him stretch out a rope to the heaven (22:15), that is, let him stretch out a rope. And it was said: the meaning is, shake towards you fresh dates upon the trunk of the palm tree. "Tusāqaṭ" means tatasāqaṭ, the tāʾ being assimilated into the sīn. Ḥamzah read "tasāqaṭ" lightened, dropping the letter which the others assimilated. ʿĀṣim, in the transmission of Ḥafṣ, read "tusāqiṭ" with u on the tāʾ, lightened, and i on the qāf. It was also read "tatasāqaṭ" with both tāʾs pronounced, and "yassāqaṭ" with yāʾ and assimilation of the tāʾ, and "tusqiṭ" and "yusqiṭ" and "tasquṭ" and "yasquṭ", with the tāʾ for the palm tree and with the yāʾ for the trunk; these are nine readings which al-Zamakhsharī (the mercy of God, Exalted, be upon him) mentioned. "Ruṭaban" is in the accusative governed by the shaking, that is: when you shake the trunk you shake down, by shaking it, fresh ripe dates. In sum, the accusative of "ruṭaban" differs according to the meanings of the readings: sometimes the verb is ascribed to the trunk, sometimes to the shaking, and sometimes to the palm tree. "Janiyyan" means that they have become good and fit for gathering; it is from janaytu al-thamarata ("I gathered the fruit"). It is related from Ibn Masʿūd, and it is not sound, that he read "it will drop upon you fresh ripe dates, barnī".{{fn:Barnī: a kind of round yellow date, reckoned the finest of dates.}} Mujāhid said of fresh ripe dates: they were ʿajwah.{{fn:A prized variety of date.}} ʿAbbās ibn al-Faḍl said: I asked Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ about His words fresh ripe dates, and he said: "which have not withered". He said: and its explanation is: they have not dried, nor become hard, nor gone far from the hands of the one gathering them; and this is the correct view. Al-Farrāʾ said: janī and majnī are one and the same, holding that the two are on a par with qatīl and maqtūl, jarīḥ and majrūḥ. Others besides al-Farrāʾ said: janī is what is cut from a single palm tree and taken from the place where it grew; and they recited:
> And the goodness of fruits in fertile meadows, and branches of trees whose gathered fruit is near at hand.

By al-janā he means what is gathered from them, that is, cut and taken. Ibn ʿAbbās said: it was a rotten trunk, and when she shook it she looked up to the top of the trunk and there were the fronds sprouting; then she looked at the spadix, which had come out from among the fronds; then it turned green and became green dates, then it reddened and became ripening dates, then fresh ripe dates, all that in the twinkling of an eye; and the fresh dates began to fall before her, none of them being bruised.

- The second: some people drew from this verse the proof that provision, though it is decreed, God, Exalted, has nonetheless entrusted the son of Adam to some effort for it, because He commanded Mary to shake the palm tree so that she might see a sign, whereas the sign could have come about without her shaking.

- The third: the command imposing the obligation of earning in the matter of provision is the way (sunnah) of God, Exalted, with His servants, and that does not impair reliance upon God (tawakkul), contrary to what the ignorant among those who affect asceticism say; this matter and the dispute about it have already been given. Before this her provision used to come to her without earning, as He said: Whenever Zachariah entered the prayer-niche to her he found provision with her (3:37), the verse. But when she gave birth she was commanded to shake the trunk. Our scholars said: when her heart was free, God freed her limbs from toil; but when she gave birth to Jesus and her heart became attached to his love, and her inmost self was occupied with talk of him and his affair, He entrusted her to her own earning and returned her to the custom of attachment to secondary causes that prevails among His servants. Al-Ṭabarī related from Ibn Zayd that Jesus (peace be upon him) said to her: "Do not grieve", and she said to him: "How should I not grieve, when you are with me, I being neither a married woman nor a slave-girl! What excuse have I before the people?! Would that I had died before this and been a thing forgotten, consigned to oblivion." And Jesus said to her: "I will suffice you for the speaking."

- The fourth: al-Rabīʿ ibn Khaytham said: in my view there is nothing better for the woman in childbed than fresh ripe dates, on account of this verse; had God known anything more excellent than fresh ripe dates for the woman in childbed, He would have fed it to Mary. For this reason they said: dates have been the custom for women in childbed from that time, and likewise the rubbing of the newborn's palate with dates (taḥnīk). And it was said: when a woman's delivery is difficult there is nothing better for her than fresh ripe dates, nor for the sick anything better than honey; al-Zamakhsharī mentioned this. Ibn Wahb said: Mālik said: God, Exalted, said fresh ripe dates; the janī among dates is what has ripened without naqsh and without spoiling. Naqsh is to prick the unripe date from below so that it softens; this is disapproved. Mālik means that this is the hastening of a thing before its time, so no one ought to do it, and if someone does it, that does not make its sale permissible, nor is it a judgement that it has ripened. This statement has already been given in al-Anʿām, and praise be to God. From Ṭalḥah ibn Sulaymān: "jiniyyan" with i on the jīm, by vowel assimilation. That is: We have put for you in the stream and the fresh dates two benefits, the first of them eating and drinking, and the second solace of the breast, since they are both miracles; and this is the meaning of His words, Exalted, so eat and drink and be comforted, that is, eat of the gathered dates and drink of the stream, and be comforted, literally "be cool of eye", at the sight of the child who is a prophet. It was read with a on the qāf, and this is the reading of the majority; al-Ṭabarī related the reading "wa-qirrī" with i on the qāf, which is the dialect of Najd. One says qarra ʿaynan yaqurru and yaqirru, with u and with i on the qāf, and aqarra Allāhu ʿaynahu fa-qarrat ("God cooled his eye and it was cooled"). It is taken from qurr and qurrah, both of which mean coldness; the tear of joy is cold and the tear of grief is hot. One party considered this weak and said: all tears are hot; so the meaning of "God cooled his eye" is that God stilled his eye by looking upon the one he loves, so that it settles and is at rest; and "so-and-so is the coolness of my eye" means my soul is at rest in his nearness. Al-Shaybānī said: and be comforted means "sleep"; He urged her to eat, drink and sleep. Abū ʿAmr said: "God cooled his eye" means He made his eye sleep and took away his sleeplessness. "ʿAynan" is in the accusative as a specification (tamyīz), as in your saying ṭib nafsan ("be of good cheer"). The action in reality belongs to the eye, but it was transferred to the possessor of the eye, and that which was in reality the agent is put in the accusative by way of explanation. Like it are ṭibtu nafsan, tafaqqaʾtu shaḥman ("I burst with fat") and taṣabbabtu ʿaraqan ("I streamed with sweat"), and the like of this is frequent.
His words, Exalted: And if you see any human being, say: I have vowed a fast to the All-Merciful (19:26). In this there are three questions:

- The first: His words, Exalted, and if you see (fa-immā tarayinna). The original form of tarayinna is tarʾayīna; the hamzah was dropped as it is dropped from tarā, and its vowel a was transferred to the rāʾ, giving tarayīna; then the first yāʾ was changed into an alif because it was vowelled and the letter before it bore a, so two unvowelled letters met, the alif changed from yāʾ and the yāʾ of the feminine; so the alif was dropped because of the meeting of two unvowelled letters, giving tarayna; then the nūn was dropped as the mark of the jussive, because in is a conditional particle and mā is an added connective, leaving taray; then the nūn of emphasis, which is doubled, was attached to it, and the yāʾ of the feminine was given i because of the meeting of two unvowelled letters, since the doubled nūn is on a par with two nūns the first of which is unvowelled, giving tarayinna. On this pattern is the saying of Ibn Durayd:
> If you see my head, its colour mimicking{{fn:The line continues: "the flight of dawn beneath the skirts of night."}}
And the saying of al-Afwah:
> If you see my head, brought low by{{fn:The line continues: "a swaggering time of reversal and despair."}}

The nūn was introduced here only by the preparatory "mā", just as the lām of the oath also prepares for its introduction. Ṭalḥah, Abū Jaʿfar and Shaybah read "tarayna" with the yāʾ unvowelled and a on a light nūn; Abū al-Fatḥ said: it is anomalous.

- The second: His words, Exalted, say: I have vowed. This is the apodosis of the condition, and there is an ellipsis in it, that is: and he asks you about your child, then say: I have vowed a fast to the All-Merciful, that is, a silence; Ibn ʿAbbās and Anas ibn Mālik said this. In the reading of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: "I have vowed to the All-Merciful a fast, a silence", and it is related from Anas.

From him also: "and a silence", with a wāw. The difference between the two wordings indicates that the word was mentioned as explanation, not as Qurʾān, and when it comes with a wāw it is possible that it is something other than the fast. What the reports from the people of ḥadīth and the transmitters of the language consistently convey is that the fast is the silence, because fasting is abstention and silence is abstention from speech. And it was said: it is the fast as commonly understood, and they were obliged to keep silent on the day of fasting except by signs; and on this the reading of Anas "and a silence", with a wāw, is explained, namely that silence was, with them, made binding in the fast by the vow, just as when one of us vows to walk to the House, that entails entering the sacred state (iḥrām) for the pilgrimage or the lesser pilgrimage. The meaning of this verse is that God, Exalted, commanded her by the tongue of Gabriel (peace be upon him), or of her son, according to the foregoing difference of opinion, to refrain from addressing human beings and to refer them to her son in this matter, so that her embarrassment might be lifted from her and the sign become manifest, and her excuse thereby stand. The evident sense of the verse is that she was permitted to say these words which are in the verse, and this is the view of the majority. One party said: the meaning of "say" is by signs, not by speech. Al-Zamakhsharī said: in it is the lesson that silence before the fool is obligatory, and among the most abject of people is a fool who finds no one to trade folly with him.

- The third: whoever binds himself by vow not to speak to any human being, it is possible to say that this is an act of devotion and so becomes binding by the vow, and it is possible to say that this is not permitted in our law because of the constriction and self-torment in it, like a vow to stand in the sun and the like. On this view the vow of silence belonged to that law, not to our law, as has already been said. Ibn Masʿūd commanded one who did that to utter speech, and this is the correct view, because of the ḥadīth of Abū Isrāʾīl which al-Bukhārī related from Ibn ʿAbbās.{{fn:Abū Isrāʾīl had vowed to stand and not sit, not to take shade, not to speak, and to fast; the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Order him to speak, to take shade and to sit, and to complete his fast."}} Ibn Zayd and al-Suddī said: the practice of fasting among them was abstention from eating and from speech. I say: and among our own practice in fasting is abstention from foul speech; he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "When one of you is fasting let him not speak obscenely nor behave ignorantly, and if someone fights him or reviles him let him say: I am fasting." And he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Whoever does not give up false speech and acting upon it, God has no need that he give up his food and his drink."

His words, Exalted: Then she brought him to her people, carrying him (19:27). It is related that when Mary was reassured by the signs she had seen, and knew that God, Exalted, would make her excuse plain, she brought him, carrying him, from the distant place to which she had withdrawn. Ibn ʿAbbās said: she went out from among them when the sun rose and came to them at noon with a child she was carrying, so the conception and the birth took place within three hours of the day. Al-Kalbī said: she gave birth where her people did not perceive her, and stayed forty days for the post-natal period, then came to her people carrying him. When they saw her with the child they grieved, for they were a righteous household, and they said in disapproval: You have indeed brought a thing farī (19:27), that is, you have brought a monstrous thing, like one who brings something he has fabricated. Mujāhid said: "fariyyan" means monstrous. Saʿīd ibn Masʿadah said: that is, invented and contrived; one says faraytu and afraytu in one and the same meaning. The child of fornication is like a fabricated thing. God, Exalted, said: nor bring a slander which they have fabricated between their hands and their feet (60:12), that is, a child whom a woman intends to attach to the husband though it is not his. One says: "so-and-so yafrī al-fariyya", that is, he does the utmost deed. Abū ʿUbaydah said: al-farī is the wonderful, the rare; al-Akhfash said this too. He said: "fariyyan" means wonderful. Fary is cutting, as though it were something that breaks through the ordinary course, or cuts short speech by its being wonderful and rare. Quṭrub said: al-farī is the new among water-skins, that is, you have brought a new thing, one in which no one has preceded you. Abū Ḥaywah read "shayʾan faryan" with the rāʾ unvowelled. Al-Suddī and Wahb ibn Munabbih said: when she brought him to her people, carrying him, the Children of Israel heard of it, and their men and women gathered; a woman stretched out her hand towards her to strike her, and God withered her side, and she was carried away in that state. Another said: "I can only think she has fornicated", and God, Exalted, struck him dumb; so the people refrained from striking her or saying to her a word that would hurt her, and began to lower their voices to her and speak gently, and they said: O Mary, you have indeed brought a thing farī, that is, monstrous. The rajaz poet said:{{fn:Zurārah ibn Ṣaʿb, answering al-ʿĀmiriyyah, who had mocked him on a journey to fetch provisions from al-Yamāmah; Ḥajr was the chief town of al-Yamāmah, and daqal is the poorest kind of date.}}
> You have fed me year-old daqal dates, weevilled, worm-eaten, from Ḥajr;
> you used to make a mighty thing of them.
That is, you used to magnify them.

His words, Exalted: O sister of Aaron (19:28). People differed about the meaning of this sisterhood and about who Aaron was. It was said: he is Aaron the brother of Moses, and the meaning is: one whom we thought the like of Aaron in worship brings the like of this! It was said: on this view Mary was of the descendants of Aaron the brother of Moses, and was linked to him by sisterhood because she was of his descendants, as one says to a Tamīmī "O brother of Tamīm" and to an Arab "O brother of the Arabs". And it was said: she had a brother on her father's side named Aaron, because this name was common among the Children of Israel, for the blessing of the name of Aaron the brother of Moses, who was the most exemplary man among the Children of Israel; al-Kalbī said this. And it was said: this Aaron was a righteous man of that time whose funeral, on the day he died, was followed by forty thousand, all of them named Aaron. Qatādah said: there was in that time among the Children of Israel a devotee wholly given over to God, Mighty and Majestic, called Aaron, and they attributed her to brotherhood with him inasmuch as she had formerly followed his way, since she was dedicated to the service of the houses of worship; that is: O you righteous woman, you were not one fit for this. Kaʿb al-Aḥbār said in the presence of ʿĀʾishah, the Mother of the Believers (may God be pleased with her), that Mary was not the sister of Aaron the brother of Moses, and ʿĀʾishah said to him: "You have lied." He said to her: "O Mother of the Believers, if the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) said it, then he is more truthful and better informed; otherwise, I find between the two of them a span of six hundred years." He said: and she fell silent. In the Ṣaḥīḥ of Muslim, from al-Mughīrah ibn Shuʿbah, who said: when I came to Najrān they questioned me and said: "You recite O sister of Aaron, yet Moses was before Jesus by such-and-such." When I came to the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) I asked him about that, and he said: "They used to name after their prophets and the righteous who were before them." In some of its lines of transmission, outside the Ṣaḥīḥ, it has come that the Christians said to him: "Your companion claims that Mary is the sister of Aaron, when there are six hundred years between them?!" Al-Mughīrah said: and I did not know what to say; and he mentioned the ḥadīth. The meaning is that it is a name which coincided with a name. From this is derived the permissibility of naming with the names of the prophets, and God knows best.

I say: the sound ḥadīth has shown that between Moses and Aaron and Jesus there was a long time. Al-Zamakhsharī said: between the two of them and him there were a thousand years or more, so it is not to be imagined that Mary was the sister of Moses and Aaron; and if it is sound, then it is as al-Suddī said, because she was of his lineage, and this is as you say to a man of a tribe: "O brother of so-and-so". From this is his saying (peace and blessings be upon him): "The brother of Ṣudāʾ has given the call to prayer, and whoever gives the call to prayer, he gives the iqāmah."{{fn:Ziyād ibn al-Ḥārith al-Ṣudāʾī, whom the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) had ordered to give the call to the dawn prayer; when Bilāl wished to give the iqāmah, the Prophet said this.}} And this is the first view. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: one party said: rather, there was in that time a profligate man named Aaron, and they attributed her to him by way of reproach and rebuke; al-Ṭabarī mentioned this without naming its author. I say: al-Ghaznawī mentioned it from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, that he was a sinner proverbial for profligacy, and she was attributed to him. The meaning is: neither your father nor your mother was one fit for this deed, so how have you brought it?! This is of the kind of insinuation (taʿrīḍ) which takes the place of explicit statement, and that, in our view, entails the prescribed punishment (ḥadd); the discussion of it will come in the sūrah of al-Nūr, if God, Exalted, wills. This last view is refuted by the sound ḥadīth, which is an explicit text, so no one has any say alongside it, and there is no dust upon it. And praise be to God. ʿUmar ibn Lajaʾ al-Taymī read: "mā kāna abāki imruʾu sawʾin" ("your father was not a man of evil").{{fn:With "your father" in the accusative as the predicate of kāna and the indefinite "a man of evil" as its noun.}}
In this there are five questions:

- The first: His words, Exalted, Then she pointed to him. They said: how can we speak to one who is in the cradle, a child? (19:29). Mary (peace be upon her) adhered to what she had been commanded, namely leaving off speech, and it is not stated in this verse that she uttered "I have vowed a fast to the All-Merciful"; it is only stated that she pointed. By this the view of those who said that her being commanded "say" meant only signs is strengthened. It is related that when she pointed to the infant they said: "Her making light of us is harder on us than her fornication." Then they said to her, by way of establishing the point: how can we speak to one who is in the cradle, a child? "Kāna" here is not intended in the sense of the past, because every single person has been a child in the cradle; rather it is in the sense of "he is now". Abū ʿUbaydah said: "kāna" here is superfluous (laghw), as the poet said:
> and neighbours of ours who were noble.{{fn:The second hemistich of a line by al-Farazdaq; the first runs: "And how, when you see the dwellings of a people".}}

And it was said: it is in the sense of existence and coming to be, as in His words and if there be one in difficulty (2:280), which has already been given. Ibn al-Anbārī said: it is not permissible to say it is redundant when it has put "ṣabiyyan" in the accusative, nor to say that "kāna" is in the sense of "came to be", because if it were in the sense of coming to be and occurring it would dispense with the predicate; you say "kāna al-ḥarr" ("the heat came") and that suffices. The correct view is that "man" is in the sense of a conditional, and "kāna" in the sense of "yakun", the implied sense being: whoever is in the cradle, a child, how shall we speak to him?! As you say: "how shall I give to one who does not accept a gift", meaning whoever does not accept. The past tense may be used in the sense of the future in a conditional, as in His words, Exalted, Blessed is He who, if He wills, will make for you better than that: gardens beneath which rivers flow (25:10), that is, if He wills He will make. And you say: "whoever has done me a kindness, from me to him is the like of it", that is, whoever does me a kindness, the like of it shall be from me to him. As for "the cradle" (al-mahd), it was said: it was a bed like a cradle; and it was said: "the cradle" here is the mother's lap; and it was said: the meaning is, how shall we speak to one whose way it is to be put to sleep in the cradle because of his smallness? When Jesus (peace be upon him) heard their words he said to them from his resting place: I am the servant of God (19:30). And this is:

- The second: it was said: Jesus (peace be upon him) was suckling, and when he heard their words he left off suckling, turned his face towards them, leaned on his left side, pointed to them with his right forefinger, and said: I am the servant of God. So the first thing he uttered was the acknowledgement of his servitude to God, Exalted, and of His lordship, as a refutation of those after him who went to extremes concerning him. The Book is the Gospel. It was said: He gave him the Book in that state, made him understand it and taught him, and gave him prophethood, as He taught Adam all the names, and he used to fast and pray. But this is exceedingly weak, as we shall explain in the question after this one. And it was said: the meaning is, He decreed for me the giving of the Book and prophethood in pre-eternity, even though the Book was not sent down at that moment; and this is the more correct.

and He has made me blessed (19:31), that is, possessed of blessings and benefits in religion and in calling to it, and a teacher of it. Al-Tustarī said: and He made me one who enjoins what is right, forbids what is wrong, guides the one who strays, aids the one wronged, and succours the distressed.

and He has enjoined upon me prayer and alms (19:31), that is, that I perform them when legal responsibility reaches me and performing them becomes possible for me, according to the latter, correct view.

as long as I live (19:31): "mā" is in the position of the accusative as an adverbial, that is, for the duration of my life. His words, Exalted: and dutiful to my mother (19:32). Ibn ʿAbbās said: when he said "and dutiful to my mother" and did not say "to my parents", it was known that he was something from God, Exalted.

and He has not made me a tyrant (19:32), that is, one who magnifies himself and is arrogant, who kills and strikes in anger. And it was said: the tyrant is the one who never acknowledges that anyone has a right over him.

wretched (19:32), that is, failing to attain good. Ibn ʿAbbās: undutiful. And it was said: disobedient to his Lord. And it was said: He did not make me one who abandons His command, so that I should be wretched as Iblīs was wretched when he abandoned His command.

- The third: Mālik ibn Anas (may God, Exalted, have mercy on him) said of this verse: how severe it is against the partisans of free will (ahl al-qadar)! Jesus (peace be upon him) told of what had been decreed of his affair, and of what would be until he died. It is related in the stories of this verse, from Ibn Zayd and others, that when they heard the words of Jesus they submitted and said: "This is indeed a mighty matter." It is related that Jesus (peace be upon him) spoke in his infancy only with this verse, then returned to the state of infants until he walked in the ordinary way of human beings, until he reached the age of boys; so his speaking was to manifest the innocence of his mother, not that he was one of those who possess understanding in that state, and it is like God's, Exalted, making the limbs speak on the Day of Resurrection. It is not transmitted that his speech continued, nor that he prayed when he was a day or a month old; and had his speech, his glorification, his preaching and his prayer continued in his childhood from the time of birth, the like of that would be something that could not be concealed. All of this indicates the unsoundness of the first view and declares plainly the ignorance of the one who holds it. It also indicates that he spoke in the cradle, contrary to the Jews and the Christians, and the proof of that is the consensus of the sects that she was not subjected to the prescribed punishment, whereas her innocence of fornication was established only by his speaking in the cradle. This verse also shows that prayer, alms and dutifulness to parents were obligatory upon the earlier communities and the bygone generations of the past, so it is among those things whose ruling stands and has not been abrogated in the law of his command. Jesus (peace be upon him) was of the utmost humility: he ate from the trees, wore hair-cloth, sat upon the dust, and sheltered wherever night overtook him, having no dwelling (peace and blessings be upon him).

- The fourth: signing is on a par with speech and conveys what speech conveys. How not, when God, Exalted, has reported of Mary and said then she pointed to him, and the people understood from her her intention and purpose, and said how can we speak. This has already been given in full in Āl ʿImrān.

- The fifth: the Kūfans said: the accusation of fornication (qadhf) by a mute is not valid, nor is his oath of imprecation (liʿān). The like is related from al-Shaʿbī, and al-Awzāʿī, Aḥmad and Isḥāq held it. In their view the accusation is valid only with the explicit word for fornication, not with its sense, and this is necessarily impossible for the mute, so he is not an accuser; nor can fornication be distinguished by signs from lawful intercourse and intercourse under a semblance of right. They said: and liʿān in our view consists of testimonies, and the testimony of the mute is not accepted, by consensus. Ibn al-Qaṣṣār said: their statement that the accusation is valid only by explicit utterance is shown false by all the other languages apart from Arabic, and so too the signs of the mute. What they mentioned of consensus regarding the testimony of the mute is an error; Mālik has stated explicitly that his testimony is accepted when his signs are understood, and that they take the place of the utterance in testimony; but where there is the ability to utter, it is not effected from him except by utterance. Ibn al-Mundhir said: those who disagree hold the mute liable in divorce, sales and all the other rulings, so the accusation ought to be like that. Al-Muhallab said: signing may be, in many chapters of jurisprudence, stronger than speech, as in his saying (peace and blessings be upon him): "I and the Hour have been sent like these two"; we know the closeness between them by the measure of the excess of the middle finger over the forefinger. And in the agreement of all minds that eye-witnessing is stronger than report there is proof that signing may in some places be stronger than speech.

And peace be upon me (19:33), that is, safety upon me from God, Exalted. Al-Zajjāj said: "peace" was mentioned before this without the definite article, so it was fitting in the second instance to mention the article. His words the day I was born, meaning in this world; and it was said: from the prodding of Satan, as has already been given in Āl ʿImrān.

and the day I die, meaning in the grave, and the day I am raised alive (19:33), meaning in the hereafter. For he has three states: in this world alive, in the grave dead, and in the hereafter raised up; so he was given peace in all his states, and this is the sense of al-Kalbī's statement. Then his speech in the cradle ceased until he reached the age of boys. Qatādah said: it was mentioned to us that a woman saw Jesus (peace be upon him) raising the dead and healing the blind and the leper, among his other signs, and she said: "Blessed is the womb that bore you and the breast that suckled you!" And Jesus (peace be upon him) said to her: "Blessed is he who recites the Book of God, Exalted, follows what is in it, and acts upon it."

His words, Exalted: That is Jesus son of Mary (19:34), that is: the one whom We have described is Jesus son of Mary, so believe this concerning him, not as the Jews say, that he was not born of a lawful union and that he was the son of Joseph the carpenter, and not as the Christians said, that he is God or the son of God.

the word of truth (19:34). Al-Kisāʾī said: "the word of truth" is a descriptive of Jesus, that is: that is Jesus son of Mary, the word of truth. He was named "the word of truth" just as he was named "the word of God", and the Truth (al-Ḥaqq) is God, Mighty and Majestic. Abū Ḥātim said: the meaning is "he is the word of truth". It has been said that the implied construction is: this speech is the word of truth. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "He means: this speech of Jesus son of Mary (peace and blessings be upon him) is the word of truth, not falsehood"; and "word" is annexed to "truth" as He said: the promise of truth which they were promised (46:16), that is, the promise and the truth; and as He said: and the abode of the Hereafter is surely better (6:32), that is, "and surely the abode, the Hereafter". ʿĀṣim and ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿĀmir read qawla l-ḥaqqi in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), that is, "I say a true saying"; and the governing element is the sense of pointing contained in That. Al-Zajjāj said: it is a verbal noun, that is, "I say the word of truth", because what precedes it points to it. It has been said that it is an accusative of praise. And it has been said that it is an accusative of incitement (ighrāʾ). ʿAbd Allāh{{fn:ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd; his reading is qāla l-ḥaqqa, "he spoke the truth".}} read qāla l-ḥaqqa. Al-Ḥasan read qūla l-ḥaqqi with a ḍammah on the qāf, and likewise in al-Anʿām qawluhu l-ḥaqqu.{{fn:Qurʾān 6:73, "His word is the truth".}} Al-qawl, al-qāl and al-qūl all have one meaning, like al-rahb, al-rahab and al-ruhb.
concerning whom (19:34) is a descriptive of Jesus.

they are in doubt (19:34), that is, they are uncertain; that is: that is Jesus son of Mary concerning whom they are in doubt, the word of truth. It has been said that they are in doubt means they differ. ʿAbd al-Razzāq mentioned: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatādah, concerning His words, Exalted, That is Jesus son of Mary, the word of truth concerning whom they are in doubt (19:34), who said: The Children of Israel gathered and brought forth from among themselves four men, each party bringing forth its learned man, and they disputed about Jesus when he was raised up. One of them said: "He is God; He came down to the earth and gave life to whom He gave life and caused to die whom He caused to die, then He ascended to heaven"; these are the Jacobites. The other three said: "You lie." Then two of them said to the third: "Speak concerning him." He said: "He is the son of God"; these are the Nestorians. The two said: "You lie." Then one of the two said to the other: "Speak concerning him." He said: "He is the third of three: God is a god, and he is a god, and his mother is a god"; these are the Isrāʾīliyyah, the kings of the Christians.{{fn:That is, the Melkites, the party of the Byzantine emperor; the name is given below as the Malkāniyyah.}} The fourth said: "You lie; rather he is the servant of God and His messenger and His spirit and His word"; these are the Muslims. Each man among them had followers who held what he said, and they fought one another, and the Muslims were overcome. That is the meaning of the words of God, Exalted: and they kill those among the people who enjoin justice (3:21). Qatādah said: and they are those of whom God, Exalted, said: Then the factions differed among themselves (19:37); they differed concerning him and became factions. This is the meaning of His words concerning whom you are in doubt with the tāʾ dotted above,{{fn:That is, tamtarūn, "you are in doubt", in the second person, instead of yamtarūn, "they are in doubt".}} which is the reading of Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī and others. Ibn ʿAbbās said: Her cousin{{fn:That is, Joseph the carpenter.}} travelled with Mary, and her son with her, to Egypt, and they remained there twelve years until the king whom they feared died. Al-Māwardī mentioned this.

I say: it occurs in the History of Egypt, in what I have seen, and it has come in the Gospel in circulation, that when the Lord Messiah was born in Bethlehem, Herod was king at that time, and that God, Exalted, revealed to Joseph the carpenter in a dream and said to him: "Arise, take the child and his mother and go to Egypt, and remain there until I tell you, for Herod is resolved to seek out Jesus to destroy him." So he rose from his sleep, obeyed the command of his Lord, took the Lord Messiah and Mary his mother, and came to Egypt. On his way to Egypt he alighted at the Well of the Balsam (Biʾr al-Balasān) which lies on the outskirts of Cairo,{{fn:At al-Maṭariyyah, the site of the "Tree of the Virgin", traditionally associated with the Holy Family's stay in Egypt.}} and she washed his garments at that well. The balsam tree springs up and grows nowhere except in that land, and from it is extracted the oil which is mixed into the oil with which the Christians baptise; for that reason a single flask of it had great value in the days of the Egyptians, and it holds a very lofty place in the esteem of the kings of the Christians, such as the king of Constantinople, the king of Sicily, the king of Abyssinia, the king of Nubia, the king of the Franks and other kings, when the kings of Egypt send it to them as a gift, and it is dearer to them than any other gift of value. On that journey the Lord Messiah reached the city of al-Ushmūnayn{{fn:Hermopolis Magna in Upper Egypt, near present-day Mallawī.}} and Qusqām,{{fn:Near al-Qūṣiyyah in the district of Manfalūṭ; the Coptic monastery there, Dayr al-Muḥarraq, is held to mark the furthest point of the Holy Family's journey.}} known now as al-Muḥarraqah, and for that reason the Christians venerate it to this day and come to it at the feast of Easter from every place, because it is the furthest point which he reached in the land of Egypt, and from it he returned to Syria. And God knows best.

His words, Exalted: It is not for God (19:35), that is, it does not befit Him and is not permissible for Him, to take any son (19:35). "Any" (min) is a connective particle in the speech, that is, "to take a son". And "to" (an) with its verb is in the position of the nominative as the subject of kāna, that is: it was not for God to take a son; that is, taking a son was never one of His attributes. Then He, Exalted, declared Himself free of what they said and said: Glory be to Him (19:35), far above having a son.
When He decrees a matter, He only says to it "Be", and it is (19:35). This has been treated exhaustively in al-Baqarah.{{fn:At Qurʾān 2:117.}}

Indeed God is my Lord and your Lord (19:36). The people of Medina, Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr read anna with fatḥah, and the people of Kufa read wa-inna with kasrah on the hamzah, taking it as the beginning of a new sentence. This is supported by the reading of Ubayy, "Be, and it is. Indeed God" without the wāw, in coordination with He said: Indeed I am the servant of God (19:30). Concerning the reading with fatḥah there are several views. The position of al-Khalīl and Sībawayh is that the meaning is "and because God is my Lord and your Lord", and likewise and that the places of prostration are for God (72:18); so anna is in the position of the accusative according to them both. Al-Farrāʾ allowed that it be in the position of the genitive by the suppression of the lām, and he also allowed that it be in the position of the genitive with the sense "and He has enjoined upon me prayer and alms as long as I live, and that God is my Lord and your Lord". Al-Kisāʾī allowed that it be in the position of the nominative with the sense "and the matter is that God is my Lord and your Lord". There is a fifth view concerning it: Abū ʿUbayd related that Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ held it, namely that the meaning is "and He decreed that God is my Lord and your Lord", so that it is coordinated with His word a matter in His words When He decrees a matter, and the meaning is: when He decrees a matter, and He decrees that God is my Lord. One may not begin recitation with anna according to this construal, nor according to the third construal; but beginning with it is permissible according to the remaining construals.
